He turns and speaks directly to the husband, to the father, to the master, and lays obligations on them. He tells husbands to love with the self-giving love of Christ. He tells fathers not to provoke their children (Ephesians 6:4). He tells masters to stop threatening and reminds them they have a Master in heaven who shows no partiality (Ephesians 6:9). In a world where power meant the absence of duty, Paul told the powerful they had duties, and grounded those duties in the God before whom the master and the slave stand equal. That is not a defense of the ancient hierarchy. It is the beginning of its unraveling, a bomb planted inside the household code with a slow fuse.

Where I land, and what I have not answered

The Constitution I write under requires that I name where I stand, the tradition it comes from, and the strongest objection I have not fully answered. I will do that, because a steelman that hides the author's own position is a dodge.

I land closer to what is usually called the mutualist or egalitarian reading, though I am not comfortable with the tribal shape those labels have taken. I believe verse 21 governs the whole passage, that mutual submission is the frame and not a preface to be discarded, that Paul's definition of headship by the cross empties the word of the domineering meaning it has been given, and that the trajectory of the passage runs toward the dignity and near-equality of the wife rather than away from it. This is a second-order question. Faithful churches divide over it, and the creeds do not bind it. A godly complementarian and a godly egalitarian are brother and sister, and I refuse to make this the wall of the faith when Scripture makes it something less.

And here is the objection I have not fully answered, stated in the form my complementarian brothers would recognize as fair. Even granting mutual submission in verse 21, Paul still gives the wife and the husband different applications of it. He does not tell husbands to submit to wives in verses 22 through 24; he tells wives to submit and husbands to love as head. The differentiation is in the text, and a reading that flattens it entirely has to explain why Paul bothered to address the two differently at all. That is a real argument. I find the cross-shaped definition of headship answers most of its force, but not all, and I would be lying to say the differentiation vanishes. It does not. I hold my position with conviction and without contempt for the brother who reads the same verses and lands a step to my right.

What submission is not, in the woman's own account

I promised a woman's perspective, and though I am a man writing it, I have listened to enough women wrestle honestly with this text to report what the faithful ones actually conclude, as against both the caricature the world paints and the distortion the abuser imposes. The women I know who submit to this passage with joy rather than fear describe something the popular debate never captures, and it is worth putting in their terms.

They say, first, that submission in Ephesians 5 is not obedience. Paul had a perfectly good word for obedience, hypakouo, and he uses it a chapter later when he tells children to obey their parents and servants to obey their masters (Ephesians 6:1, 5). He does not use it for wives. He uses hypotasso, to place oneself in order under, a word with a voluntary and self-giving quality that the word for obedience lacks. A wife is never told to obey her husband in this passage. She is invited to a freely chosen yielding, which is a categorically different thing than the commanded obedience of a child or a slave, and the difference is not a technicality. A woman who is commanded is a subordinate. A woman who freely places herself is a partner performing an act of love, and an act of love that is coerced is not love at all.

They say, second, that the submission is bounded by the object of ultimate loyalty. "Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord" (Ephesians 5:22). The phrase "as to the Lord" is not a way of making the husband a stand-in for God. It is the opposite. It subordinates the whole arrangement to a prior and higher allegiance. A wife submits to her husband within her submission to the Lord, which means the moment a husband asks her to sin, to violate her conscience, to betray Christ, the ordering collapses, because her deepest submission was never to him. Peter and John set the principle for every Christian when they said, "We must obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29), and no marriage text overrides it. A submission that has no such limit is not the Christian kind. It is idolatry with a ring on.

They say, third, that they have never once found this text a burden when it was matched by a husband living out verses 25 through 33. The whole thing works, they tell me, or fails, on whether the man is dying. A wife's yielding to a husband who is laying down his life for her, studying her, honoring her, nourishing her as his own body, is not a hardship; it is the natural response to being loved that thoroughly. The passage was never meant to be read one clause at a time by parties looking to extract their advantage. It was meant to describe a mutual self-donation in which each gives the other more than the other could demand. The tragedy is not the text. The tragedy is every marriage in which one half of it was obeyed and the other half was not.

The verdict

Here is what I will not soften, because a woman who has been hit with this text deserves at least this much clarity.

Whatever submission means in Ephesians 5, it cannot mean what the abuser needs it to mean. A husband who uses this passage to demand, to control, to dominate, to silence, or to strike has not read past verse 22, and he has certainly not read verse 25. He has taken a text about a love that goes to the cross and turned it into a warrant for a power the text explicitly forbids him. He is not obeying the passage. He is inverting it. The very verses he quotes to justify his authority are the verses that condemn him, because they command him to a crucified love and he has chosen a crown instead.

To the woman who circled that word in fear, I want to say the thing the church too often did not: the God who wrote that passage is not on the side of the man crushing you with it. The passage begins with mutual submission and defines the husband's role by a Savior who let himself be killed rather than lift a hand against his bride. If your marriage looks like the opposite of Calvary, the problem is not that you have submitted too little. The problem is that no one has loved you the way the passage demands, and the text you have been beaten with is the very text that was meant to protect you.

We handed men half a sentence and called it the will of God. The other half is still there, on the page, in the Greek, waiting for a church honest enough to read it out loud.

chapters.title: Marriage Through Depression and Crisis
chapters.summary: When one of you goes dark, the vow stops being a feeling and becomes a structure, and the structure is the only thing that holds when the feeling is gone.
chapters.body:
There comes a season in many marriages when one of you goes dark. Not difficult. Dark. A depression that flattens the person you married into someone who cannot get off the couch, cannot feel the love you are offering, cannot say why, cannot promise it will lift. Or a crisis crashes in from outside, a diagnosis, a lost job that takes a man's sense of himself with it, a child in trouble, a grief that does not have an end date. And the marriage that worked when both of you were well discovers it has to learn an entirely different way to function, because one of the two people holding it up has, for now, let go of the rope.

I have walked through dark seasons in my own life and I have sat with too many couples in theirs, and I want to say some honest things, because the church often handles this terribly, reaching for a verse like a bandage over a wound that needs surgery.

First, the depressed spouse is not choosing this and cannot simply choose their way out, and a marriage that treats depression as a failure of will or faith will pour shame onto a person already drowning in it. Depression is not sadness and it is not a bad attitude and it is very often not even about anything, which is the cruelest part, because the well spouse keeps trying to fix the cause and there is no cause to fix. The illness lies to the person who has it. It tells them they are a burden, that their family would be better off without them, that they have always been like this and always will be, that the love around them is not real or is not for them. None of it is true and all of it feels truer than anything they have ever known. If you are married to someone in this, your first job is to refuse to believe the illness's account of your spouse, and to keep telling them the truth they cannot feel, knowing the words may not land, saying them anyway, because someday the fog will lift and they will need to have heard them.

Let me say the thing the church will not. Get the help. Real help. A doctor, a counselor, medication if it is called for, and I will not let anyone shame a brother or sister for taking it. The notion that a faithful Christian should be able to pray their way out of clinical depression has killed people, and I mean that literally. We do not tell the diabetic that insulin shows a lack of faith. The brain is an organ. Sometimes it gets sick. Treating it is not unbelief, it is stewardship of the body God gave you, and the spouse who gently insists on real treatment, who makes the appointment, who goes along, is doing one of the most loving things a marriage allows. Prayer and a doctor are not rivals. Take both.

Now the harder, lonelier truth, the one for the well spouse, because there is a special grief that no one warns you about, which is the grief of being married to someone who is alive but absent. You are not a widow and you are not divorced, but the person you married is somewhere you cannot reach, and the marriage gives you nothing back for a long time, and you are exhausted and you are lonely and you feel guilty for being either because they are the one who is suffering. Hear me. Your suffering is real too. Caring for a depressed or sick spouse is one of the heaviest loads a human being carries, and carrying it does not make your own depletion selfish. You cannot pour from a dry well for years and stay standing. You need your own support, your own people, your own help, and getting it is not abandonment, it is the only way you survive long enough to be there when the season turns.

This is where the vow stops being a feeling and becomes a structure, and the structure is the entire point. When we marry, we promise in sickness and in health, for better and for worse, and we say the words on the best day of our lives when the worse is unimaginable. The words are not for that day. The words are for this one. The vow is precisely the thing that holds the marriage together when the feelings that usually hold it have gone silent, and a marriage built only on feeling will not survive the season when one person cannot feel anything at all. The covenant is load-bearing. It carries the weight the emotions used to carry, and the discovery that it can, that the promise holds when nothing else does, is one of the few mercies hidden inside a dark season. You learn what your vow was actually made of, and you find out it was made of something stronger than your mood.

Let me steel-man the spouse at the edge of leaving, because I have sat with them and I will not pretend the case is weak. You might say, I did not sign up for this, the person I married is gone, it has been years, I am withering, and surely God does not require me to disappear into someone else's illness forever. I want to honor how much pain is in that, and I want to refuse the easy answer in both directions. I will not tell you that leaving is always sin, because there are situations, untreated and dangerous, abusive, where staying is not faithfulness but destruction, and you are not required to be destroyed. But I will tell you this. Depression and crisis are seasons far more often than they are life sentences, and the spouse who leaves in the dark of it frequently leaves just before the dawn they could not see coming, and carries the leaving forever. Before you decide the person is gone, make sure you fought for them the way you would want to be fought for if it were you in the dark, because someday it may be, and the way you treat your spouse in their worst season is the sermon you are preaching to yourself about what your own worst season will hold.

There is also a strange grace that the church almost never names, which is what these seasons make of the well spouse. To love someone who cannot love you back, to keep returning to a person who gives you nothing in return, to serve without reciprocity for a long time, is the closest most of us will ever come to loving the way God loves us. He loved us while we were dead, Paul says, dead, giving nothing back, unable even to reach for him. The well spouse in a dark season is being conformed to that love, ground into a shape they would never have chosen, and the love that comes out the other side is not the eager love of the wedding day, it is something deeper and more terrible and more like the real thing, a love that has been tested against an empty room and did not leave.

And to the one in the dark, if you are the one who cannot feel it, hear this. You are not a burden, whatever the illness tells you. Your worth does not run on your usefulness, and the love around you is not a debt you have failed to pay. Stay. Get the help. Let the people who love you carry you through the part where you cannot carry yourself, because that is what the carrying is for, and someday the fog will thin and you will be able to receive again what was given to you in the dark, and you will find it was real the whole time. The marriage held while you could not. That is not your failure. That is the covenant doing the exact thing it was made to do.

Weeping may last for the night, the psalm says, but joy comes in the morning. It does not say how long the night is. Some nights in a marriage are years long. The promise is not that the night is short. The promise is that there is a morning, and that the God who keeps the marriage through the dark is the same God who is bringing the dawn, even when no one in the house can see it yet.

chapters.title: Men and Marriage: Why Husbands Check Out
chapters.summary: The husband who has emotionally left the marriage rarely announces it. He simply grows quieter, more distant, more absent while still present. And there are reasons, none of them excuses.
chapters.body:
There is a particular kind of dead marriage that does not involve any dramatic betrayal, any affair, any single event you could point to. The husband is still there. He comes home, he provides, he is not cruel. But somewhere along the way he left, in every way that matters, while continuing to physically occupy the house. His wife lives with a man who is present and absent at once, and she cannot name the loss because nothing technically happened, and he cannot see the loss because from the inside it does not feel like leaving. It feels like coping. I want to talk about the husband who has checked out, why it happens, and why understanding it is the first step to reversing it.

The slow drift no one chooses

No man decides to check out of his marriage. That is the first thing to understand, and it matters for both grace and diagnosis. The checked out husband did not sit down one day and resolve to withdraw his heart. He drifted, by degrees so small that no single day registered as a departure, until one day the distance was simply the water he swam in and he could not remember the country he had left.

It usually begins with conflict he does not know how to handle. Something is wrong between them, and she wants to talk about it, and talking about it means entering emotional territory he has no map for, because, as we have said elsewhere, he was never given the tools to navigate his own interior, let alone hers. The conversation goes badly. He feels attacked, or he feels the crushing sense of failing at something he does not understand, and both of those feelings are unbearable to him. So the next time conflict looms, he does the thing that brings immediate relief. He withdraws. He goes quiet, he goes to the garage, he goes into the phone, he changes the subject. And the withdrawal works, in the short term, the way all avoidance works. The unbearable feeling recedes.

No husband decides to leave his marriage while staying in the house. He simply discovers, one avoided conversation at a time, that he already has.

Why withdrawal feels like survival

To the man, withdrawal does not feel like abandonment. It feels like self protection, even like keeping the peace. There is often a physiological piece to this that we do not talk about enough. When conflict escalates, many men experience a kind of internal flooding, a stress response that makes them feel overwhelmed and shuts down their capacity to think and speak. In that state the man is not being cold on purpose. He is drowning, and withdrawal is him coming up for air. The problem is that what feels like coming up for air to him feels like being abandoned to her, and both experiences are real, and neither can see the other's.

Over years, this pattern hardens into a whole way of being married. He learns that the way to handle a difficult wife is to endure and withdraw. She learns that the way to reach an absent husband is to pursue harder, which floods him more, which makes him withdraw further, which makes her pursue more desperately, a terrible machine that runs on its own momentum and grinds the marriage down. He experiences her as relentlessly critical. She experiences him as a stone wall. Both are right about their experience and both are wrong about the other's heart, and the machine keeps running because neither knows how to stop it.

The stories he tells himself

As the distance grows, the husband builds stories to explain it, and the stories protect him from having to change. The most common is that his wife is simply impossible, too emotional, never satisfied, always finding fault, so that any reasonable man would keep his head down. There is often a grain of truth, and the grain is what makes the story stick, but the story conveniently locates the entire problem outside himself and requires nothing of him. It is a comfortable story because it makes his withdrawal her fault.

Another story is that this is just what marriage becomes, that the early closeness was always going to fade, that everyone's marriage goes flat eventually, and so his particular deadness is nothing unusual and nothing to fight against. This story counsels resignation and calls it realism. It lets him grieve nothing and change nothing, because if all marriages die then his is not really dying, it is just aging normally, and there is nothing to be done.

The story that his wife is impossible is comfortable precisely because it is the one story that asks nothing of him.

These stories are powerful because each contains enough truth to be believable. His wife may in fact be critical. Marriages do in fact cool. He is in fact tired. But a partial truth deployed to avoid responsibility becomes a lie, and the function of all three stories is identical, to explain the man's absence in a way that requires nothing of him and locates the problem anywhere but in his own heart. As long as he believes any of them, he will not change, because the stories exist precisely to make change seem unnecessary.

And there is the busiest story, which is simply busyness itself. The man fills his life so completely with work and tasks and the endless demands of provision that there is genuinely no space left for the marriage, and he can tell himself, truthfully, that he is exhausted, that he has nothing left at the end of the day. What he does not examine is that the busyness is not entirely accidental. Some of it is a flight. It is easier to be exhausted by work than to sit in the hard silence of a marriage that has grown cold, and so the man unconsciously keeps himself too busy to have to face it.

What it takes to come back

So how does a checked out husband come back, if he wants to, and if his wife has not entirely given up waiting. It begins with the man owning his part without waiting for her to change first. This is the crucial and the hardest move. Every instinct in him wants to make his return conditional, wants to say he will re engage when she stops being critical, when she makes it safe, when she meets him halfway. But the man is called, by the pattern of Christ, to love first and to move first, to give himself for her as Christ gave himself for the church, which was not a response to the church's loveliness but the cause of it.

Practically, coming back means learning to stay in the room. It means recognizing the flooding when it starts and, instead of walking out, saying something honest like, I am overwhelmed and I need a few minutes, but I am not leaving this, I will come back to it. That single sentence, the promise to return, changes everything, because it distinguishes a pause from an abandonment. It means letting her back into his interior, which requires him to first find his interior, which is the long slow work of a man learning to feel and name what is actually happening inside him.

What she is actually asking for

Part of what keeps a husband checked out is a fundamental misreading of what his wife is asking. He hears her requests for connection as demands to be met, problems to be solved, criticisms to be defended against, and he responds accordingly, either by trying to fix the thing she named or by retreating from the perceived attack. In both cases he has missed her entirely, because she was not mainly asking him to fix anything or attacking anything. She was asking to be close to him, and connection was the whole point.

When a wife says she feels alone, the checked out husband often responds by listing the ways he has been present, the provision, the faithfulness, the tasks completed, as though she had made an accusation he must rebut. But she was not keeping a ledger of his failures. She was reaching for him, and his defensive accounting is itself another form of the withdrawal, another way of not being emotionally present in the moment she most needs him to be. He answered the words and missed the person, and she feels lonelier than before, because now she has been reached for and met with a spreadsheet.

The husband who wants to come back has to learn a new way of hearing his wife, one that listens underneath the words for the reach that is almost always there. When she raises a concern, the deepest question is usually not can you fix this but are you with me, do you see me, will you turn toward me instead of away. And the answer she needs is not a solution but his presence, his turning toward her, his willingness to stay in the difficult moment and be emotionally with her in it. That turning toward, repeated over time, is how the machine of pursuit and withdrawal finally stops, because she no longer has to pursue a man who is already moving in her direction.

The cost of waiting too long

I have to be honest about a hard reality, because false comfort helps no one. Sometimes a husband checks out for so long that his wife, after years of reaching for a man who kept withdrawing, finally stops reaching. She protects herself. She builds her life around his absence and quietly grieves the marriage she is technically still in. And here is the cruel irony that I have watched play out more than once. It is often at this point, when she has finally given up and gone quiet, that the husband first notices something is wrong, because the pursuit he found so exhausting has stopped, and its absence unsettles him more than its presence ever did.

The man who waits until his wife stops reaching has waited dangerously long, because a heart that has protected itself against years of withdrawal does not immediately reopen the moment the husband decides to come back. She has learned, through painful repetition, that reaching for him leads to being hurt, and that lesson is written deep, and it does not unwrite itself just because he has finally shown up. His return, when it comes this late, will require a patience he is not used to, a willingness to keep turning toward her even when she cannot yet trust it, to prove over a long time that the change is real and not another false start.

It is often when a wife finally stops reaching that the husband first notices anything is wrong. By then, his return will cost far more than his presence ever would have.

And I want to add a word of hope even for the man who has waited too long, whose wife has already gone quiet, because I have seen even those marriages come back. The coming back is slower and it costs the husband more, but it is not impossible, and the God who raises the dead is not intimidated by a marriage that looks like a corpse. What it requires of the man is a patience proportional to the years of his absence, a willingness to keep turning toward a wife who cannot yet trust the turning, to prove the change across a long enough stretch that her protected heart can finally believe it is safe to hope again. That is a demanding road, but it is a road, and a man who committed the long slow damage can undertake the long slow repair, and grace has walked that road with men I know.

So the word to the drifting husband is one of urgency. Do not wait until the pursuit stops to conclude the marriage was fine. The pursuit was the evidence that she still hoped, and its persistence, exhausting as it felt, was a gift. The time to turn around is now, while she is still reaching, while the distance is still crossable, before the years of withdrawal have taught her to protect herself against you. A marriage can come back from almost anywhere, but the coming back is easier the sooner it begins, and the man who understands this will not let one more year pass in the drift, telling himself there is time, when the whole tragedy of the checked out husband is that he always believed there was time and only discovered otherwise when it had nearly run out.

And it means letting go of the self justifying stories, the impossible wife and the naturally dying marriage and the innocent busyness, and telling himself a truer and more costly story, which is that he has been absent, that his absence has wounded someone he vowed to love, and that no one is coming to fix this for him. I write this as a husband who has caught himself in the garage, in the phone, in the too full schedule, choosing the relief of distance over the harder work of presence. The drift is real and it is powerful and no marriage is immune to it. But it is a drift, not a sentence, and a man who is willing to stop drifting, to turn around and swim back toward his wife across the distance he did not mean to create, will often find that she has been standing on the far shore the whole time, exhausted from waiting, and still hoping he would come.

chapters.title: Military Marriage: Distance, Deployment, and Covenant
chapters.summary: The marriage that survives deployment does not merely endure distance. It learns to carry a weight that most civilian marriages never have to name.
chapters.body:
The phone call comes at 0200 and the line is bad. There is a three-second delay that makes conversation feel like speaking across a canyon. You say "I love you" and wait. The silence stretches. Then the voice comes back, thin and far away: "I love you too." And you both know that the words are true and that the words are not enough and that the words are all you have.

Military marriage exists in a category the church has never adequately addressed. It is not merely a marriage under stress — all marriages face stress. It is a marriage in which the state has a prior claim on one spouse's body, time, location, and availability. The service member did not simply take a job with long hours. They swore an oath that supersedes every other obligation except the oath they swore at the altar, and the two oaths exist in a tension that no amount of patriotic sentiment can resolve.

I have sat across from military couples in my office — young men and women who married at twenty-one because deployment was coming and they wanted to be married before they left, who came home to find that the person they married had become someone they did not recognize, or who discovered that they themselves had become someone their spouse could not reach. The divorce rate among military families tells part of the story. The rest of the story sits in the silences of couples who stayed together but lost something they cannot name.

The Covenant Under Competing Oaths

Every military spouse eventually confronts a question the church rarely helps them articulate: What does it mean to be in covenant with someone who has sworn a prior oath to a nation? The marriage vow says "forsaking all others." The military oath says "I will support and defend the Constitution of the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic." Both are sacred. Both demand everything. And when they conflict — when the deployment comes during the pregnancy, when the reassignment uproots the family for the fourth time, when the midnight call means leaving the dinner table mid-sentence — the military oath almost always wins.

This is not a betrayal. The spouse who serves did not break their marriage vow by honoring their military oath. But the marriage absorbs the cost of that honoring, and the cost is real. The cost is birthdays missed and anniversaries spent alone. The cost is single parenting for months at a stretch, making every decision about the house and the children and the bills without the partner who promised to share them. The cost is the slow erosion of shared experience — the inside jokes that fade, the daily rhythms that diverge, the growing awareness that you and your spouse are living in different worlds and calling it one marriage.

The church has mostly responded to military marriage with gratitude and admiration, which is appropriate but insufficient. Gratitude does not help at 0200 when the baby is screaming and the spouse is on the other side of the world. Admiration does not speak to the anger — the entirely legitimate anger — that surfaces when a service member comes home and expects the household to reorganize around their presence, as if the family had been on pause rather than in motion.

What Deployment Does to the One Who Stays

The spouse who stays home during deployment undergoes a transformation that is rarely acknowledged and almost never theologically engaged. They become, in effect, a single parent with a married person's obligations. They manage the household, raise the children, handle the finances, maintain the property, navigate the military bureaucracy, and do it all while carrying an ambient dread that the next knock on the door might be the one that changes everything.

Over time, the staying spouse develops competence, independence, and decision-making authority that the deployed spouse did not see emerging. This is not a problem; it is a survival mechanism. But when the deployed spouse returns, the competence that kept the family afloat during their absence can feel like a threat. The spouse who stayed has learned to function without them. The spouse who returns has to find their place in a household that learned to run without them.

This reintegration — the return — is often harder than the deployment itself. The deployment has a narrative: separation, endurance, reunion. The reintegration has no narrative. It is the daily, undramatic, exhausting work of two people learning to share a life again after months of living separate ones. It is the fight about where the dishes go, because the staying spouse rearranged the kitchen. It is the tension at bedtime, because the children have a routine with one parent and the other parent does not know it. It is the sex that is supposed to be a reunion but feels like an audition.

The church can name this. The church should name this. Reintegration is not a homecoming party and a thank-you-for-your-service. It is a covenant being renegotiated in real time, and both spouses need the church to say: this is normal. This is hard. You are not failing.

What Deployment Does to the One Who Goes

The service member who deploys carries a burden the church is even less equipped to address. They live in an environment that demands hypervigilance, hierarchy, and emotional compression. They see things — or do things — that cannot be translated into the language of home. They develop relationships with fellow service members that are forged in a furnace of shared danger, and those relationships have an intensity that marriage, by its very domesticity, cannot replicate.

I do not mean that the deployed spouse loves their unit more than their family. I mean that the deployed spouse experiences a form of intimacy — the intimacy of shared risk — that their spouse at home cannot access. And when they come home, they carry the guilt of that intimacy along with everything else they carry. They wonder why the bond with their battle buddy feels more real than the bond with their spouse. They wonder what it says about them that they miss the deployment — not the danger, but the clarity, the purpose, the knowledge of exactly who they were and what they were supposed to do.

The church has a word for what the returning service member experiences, though it rarely uses it in this context. The word is exile. The service member returns to a home that is still their home but no longer feels like it. The furniture is the same. The family is the same. But something has shifted — in them, in the household, in the space between — and the shift cannot be undone by simply being present.

The Psalms of ascent — those songs the Israelites sang as they climbed toward Jerusalem after exile — know this feeling. "When the Lord restored the fortunes of Zion, we were like those who dream." The return from exile does not feel like arrival. It feels like dreaming. The military spouse who comes home and sits on their own couch and feels, inexplicably, like a stranger — that person needs to hear that they are not broken. They are in exile, and exile is a biblical category, and God meets people there.

The Children Between Two Worlds

Military children learn early that home is not a place. It is a relationship that moves. They change schools every two or three years. They make friends knowing they will leave them. They develop a resilience that adults admire and a rootlessness that adults underestimate. The phrase "military brat" carries a strange pride, but it also carries a grief that many military children do not have permission to express — the grief of never quite belonging anywhere, of always being the new kid, of loving a parent who keeps leaving.

The church that serves military families must take these children seriously. Not as props for patriotic Sundays. Not as illustrations of sacrifice. As people — young people who are carrying a weight they did not choose and who need a community that will still be there after the next reassignment. The most powerful thing a church near a military base can do is not hold a special service on Veterans Day. It is to know the names of the children, to remember them after they move, to be the stable presence in a life defined by instability.

Toward a Theology of Military Marriage

A theology adequate to military marriage would need to hold several tensions simultaneously. It would need to honor service without idolizing it. It would need to acknowledge sacrifice without romanticizing it. It would need to name the real costs — to marriages, to children, to mental health, to faith itself — without undermining the legitimacy of the call to serve.

It would also need to reckon with the moral complexity that military service introduces into a marriage. The spouse who serves may be ordered to do things that trouble their conscience. The spouse who stays may carry a moral weight — complicity by association, pride tangled with dread — that the church's categories of sin and righteousness cannot easily sort. These are not theoretical concerns. They are the concerns of real people in real marriages, and the church's silence on them is a pastoral failure.

What military marriage teaches — what it teaches all of us, if we are willing to learn — is that covenant is not sustained by proximity. It is sustained by fidelity in the absence of proximity. The military couple who stays married through three deployments has learned something about covenant that the couple who has never spent a night apart cannot know. They have learned that love is not a feeling sustained by presence. It is a decision renewed in absence. It is the letter written at midnight. It is the prayer offered across time zones. It is the choice, made again and again, to remain married to someone you cannot see, cannot touch, cannot hear except through a bad phone line with a three-second delay.

That is not a diminished form of marriage. It is marriage refined by fire. And the church should say so — not on Veterans Day, not in a special bulletin insert, but in its regular theology of marriage, in its sermons and its counseling and its understanding of what covenant looks like when it costs everything it promises.

The military family in your congregation does not need your admiration. They have plenty of that. They need your theology. They need to know that the God who sustains covenant is present in the distance and the deployment and the 0200 phone call. They need to know that the church sees them — not as heroes, not as victims, but as married people doing the hardest version of a hard thing.

They need to know they are not alone. Even when they are.

chapters.title: Money and Marriage
chapters.summary: Money fights are almost never about money, they are about fear and control and worth, and a budget cannot fix a thing the budget cannot see.
chapters.body:
When couples come to me about money, they think they are coming about money. They have the numbers ready. They want me to adjudicate, to look at the spending and tell the other one they are wrong. And I have learned to set the numbers aside almost immediately, because in fifteen years of these conversations I have rarely met a money fight that was actually about money. The money is the surface. Underneath it, every time, is something older and more tender. Fear. Control. Worth. The childhood that taught you what money means and whether there will ever be enough.

You marry not just a person but a whole financial history you cannot see. One of you grew up watching the lights get shut off, and now a low balance does not register as a number, it registers as terror, the body remembering a cold house. The other grew up where money was always there and never discussed, and now the spouse's anxiety reads as irrational, controlling, no fun. Neither of you is being unreasonable given where you came from. You are being faithful to two different gods of money you were each handed before you could choose, and you brought both of those gods into the same house and the same account, and now they are at war and you think you are just disagreeing about a vacation.

So the first work is not budgeting. It is testimony. You sit down, not in a fight, and you tell each other the truth about money. What did money feel like in the house you grew up in. What were you afraid of. What did your father do with it, your mother, and what did it teach you to expect. I have watched this single conversation do more for a marriage's finances than any spreadsheet, because once a man understands that his wife's frugality is a six-year-old standing in a cold house, he stops fighting the frugality and starts comforting the child. And once she understands that his generosity is a wound too, a need to never be the man who had nothing to give, she stops calling him careless and starts seeing the fear under the open hand.

Now let me be practical, because the testimony without structure is just feelings, and money does not respond to feelings. It responds to decisions.

The single most important financial decision a married couple makes is whether the money is ours. Not legally, that is settled the day you marry. I mean in the heart, in the daily practice. There is a way of running a marriage's finances that keeps a quiet wall down the middle, your money and my money, your bills and mine, a careful ledger of who paid for what. I understand why people do it. It feels safe, especially for someone who has been financially burned before, and especially for a spouse who earns less and does not want to feel like they are asking for an allowance. But that wall is a contract wall, and a covenant has no wall. The biblical picture of marriage is one flesh, and one flesh does not run two accounts and keep score. The practice has to match the promise. If you have pledged your whole self to this person, the money is part of the self you pledged.

This cuts hard against something the culture says is just prudent. Keep your own account, just in case. Protect yourself. And I want to honor the real fear in that, because there are marriages where one spouse is genuinely reckless or genuinely abusive, and protecting yourself is wisdom and not faithlessness. I am not telling a woman married to a man who gambles the rent to hand him the keys to everything. That is not covenant, that is enabling, and they are different. But for most couples the separate-accounts instinct is not protecting against a real danger. It is keeping a door cracked toward the exit, a quiet hedge that says I have not fully bet on this. And the marriage feels that hedge even when no one names it. You cannot be all-in on a person while keeping a private bunker. The bunker is a message, and the message is, I am not sure about you.

Then there is the question of who controls the spending, and this is where most of the daily friction lives. Hear me. One person tracking the budget is fine. One person being the family's controller, having to approve the other's every purchase like a parent doling out lunch money, is not stewardship. It is a slow humiliation, and it is especially cruel when it lands on the spouse who earns less or stays home, because it tells them their work has no monetary dignity. If your spouse cannot buy a coffee or a book without filing a request, you do not have a budget. You have a hierarchy, and you have made yourself the throne. The fix is a shared plan with room in it for each person to be a free adult. You decide together what the categories are, and then within reason each of you gets to be trusted. Trust is not a reward for good behavior. It is the air a marriage breathes.

Let me name the harder cases honestly. Debt is the one that hides. A spouse opens a card, then another, covers the minimums, says nothing, and the shame of the first lie funds the second, and by the time it surfaces the betrayal is not really about the dollars, it is about the months of looking you in the eye and hiding. Financial infidelity is a real category and the church almost never talks about it, but I have watched it break trust as deeply as the other kind. If you are hiding money or hiding debt from your spouse, the dollars are not your worst problem. The hiding is. And the only way out is the way that costs you, which is to bring it into the light before you are caught, to say the number out loud, the whole number, and to let your spouse be angry without rushing them past it. The relief on the other side of confession is real, but you do not get the relief without the confession, and there is no version where you keep the secret and keep the marriage whole.

There is another fault line that runs through more marriages than couples admit, which is the gap between the earner and the one who earns less or earns nothing in dollars. In a culture that measures a person by their paycheck, the spouse who stays home with children, or whose work is unpaid, or who simply makes less, can absorb a quiet message that their contribution counts for less, and that message poisons everything. It shows up in who feels entitled to spend, in whose preferences win, in the subtle posture of the higher earner as the one doing the family a favor. This is a lie, and it is a lie the gospel directly contradicts, because the kingdom of God does not rank people by their productivity, and a marriage that secretly does is running on the world's scoreboard and not on Christ's. The woman raising five children is not a dependent. She is doing work that no salary could cover and that the family could not survive without. The husband whose business failed is not worth less than the wife whose career is climbing. If money has become the measure of worth in your house, you have a deeper problem than the budget, and it will surface as resentment long before it surfaces as a number.

And then there is the deepest thing, the thing money is always quietly asking, which is, what do we actually live for. A budget is a moral document whether you intend it to be or not. It is a record of what you worshiped, written in dollars, with no power to lie. You can tell me your priorities, and then I can read your statements, and the statements will tell me the truth. So a married couple has to decide together, not just how to spend, but what the money is for. Is it for security, for status, for the kids' every advantage, for a house that announces something to the neighbors. Or is it held a little loosely, in open hands, with generosity built into the plan before the wants get their turn. The couples I have watched stay free around money are not the ones with the most of it. They are the ones who decided early that the money serves the marriage and the mission, and not the other way around, and who put that decision into the actual numbers where it could be tested.

Jesus said more about money than about heaven or hell, and he said it because he knew the human heart attaches itself to money the way it should attach itself to God. You cannot serve both, he said, naming money almost as a rival deity, which is exactly how it functions in a marriage. So the real work is not financial. It is whether two people can hold money together with open hands, telling each other the truth, refusing the secret accounts and the secret debts and the quiet thrones, and deciding together what their one shared life is actually for. Do that, and the budget mostly takes care of itself. Skip it, and no spreadsheet will save you, because you were never fighting about money in the first place.

chapters.title: Money and Marriage: Why It's Always About More Than Money
chapters.summary: Every fight about money is a fight about something else — about security, about control, about the stories you absorbed before you were old enough to question them — and until you name the something else, the money fights will never end.
chapters.body:
In fifteen years of pastoral ministry, I have never seen a couple fight about money. I have seen them fight about what money represents — security, freedom, control, identity, the fear of becoming their parents, the fear of failing their children — but never about money itself. Money is the surface. It is always the surface. And the couples who spend their energy arguing about the surface never get to the substance underneath, which is why the arguments recur with such depressing regularity. You cannot resolve a conflict you have not correctly diagnosed.

The research confirms what pastoral experience suggests. A study published in "Family Relations" by Sonya Britt-Lutter and colleagues found that arguments about money are the top predictor of divorce — more than arguments about sex, parenting, or in-laws. But the same research found that the predictive power was not about the amount of money. Couples with high incomes fought about money with the same intensity and frequency as couples with low incomes. The variable was not the balance in the account. It was the meaning assigned to the balance. And meaning, as every theologian knows, is where the real battles are fought.

I have five sons. I grew up without a father. The intersection of those two facts means that my relationship with money is shaped by scarcity and responsibility in ways I did not understand for most of my adult life. I provided fiercely because I had not been provided for. I worried obsessively because worry felt like vigilance, and vigilance felt like love. It took years — and a wife who refused to accept my anxiety as virtue — to see that the money story I was living was not a financial plan. It was a wound wearing a suit.

The Money Stories You Inherited

Before you ever opened a joint checking account, you had a money story. It was written for you in childhood, by parents and circumstances you did not choose, and it was inscribed so deeply into your operating system that by the time you married, you did not even know it was there. You thought you were just being "responsible" or "generous" or "careful." You were actually enacting a script that was written decades ago, in a household you no longer live in, by people whose financial anxieties became your own.

The child who grew up in poverty carries a particular relationship with money into adulthood. Money is scarce. Money can disappear. Money must be hoarded, protected, worried over. Every purchase is a risk. Every expenditure is a potential catastrophe. The adult who carries this story may have a six-figure income and a full savings account and still feel the anxiety of the child who watched the power get shut off. The rational brain knows the bills are paid. The child brain does not trust it.

The child who grew up in affluence carries a different relationship. Money is available. Money is a tool. Money solves problems. The adult who carries this story may spend freely, give generously, and feel genuinely confused when their spouse panics about the credit card statement. They are not being irresponsible. They are living inside a story in which money is not a source of fear.

When these two stories marry each other — and they frequently do, because opposites attract precisely because they compensate for each other's anxiety — the result is a conflict that neither party can resolve by argument, because the conflict is not about the current expenditure. It is about the childhood wound that the expenditure has activated. He sees a dining room table she wants to buy and feels the panic of a child whose family could not afford furniture. She sees a savings account he obsesses over and feels the suffocation of a child whose family's frugality was actually control. Both are responding to the present through the lens of the past, and neither knows it.

The first step in resolving money conflicts in marriage is not a better budget. It is a better autobiography. Each spouse must tell the story of money as they experienced it growing up — not the financial details, but the emotional reality. What did money feel like in your home? Was it discussed openly or hidden? Was it a source of anxiety or a source of freedom? What was the worst money moment of your childhood? What did you swear you would never repeat? These questions do not appear in any financial planning software. They are more important than any spreadsheet.

The Four Money Personalities

Financial counselors and researchers have identified broad patterns in how individuals relate to money. The specific taxonomies vary, but the general categories are consistent across the literature. Savers hoard. Spenders deploy. Avoiders refuse to engage. Risk-takers gamble on future returns. Every person carries a primary orientation, and every marriage involves the collision of two orientations that are almost never the same.

The saver-spender marriage is the most common combination and the most volatile. The saver sees the spender as reckless, irresponsible, a threat to the family's stability. The spender sees the saver as controlling, fearful, unwilling to enjoy the resources they have worked to earn. Both are partially right. Both are projecting their own money story onto their spouse's behavior. And the argument about whether to take the vacation or add to the emergency fund is never, ever about the vacation or the emergency fund. It is about two competing visions of what money is for, rooted in two different childhoods, expressing two different fears.

The avoider-engaged marriage is less volatile but equally damaging. One spouse handles the finances. The other checks out — does not look at the statements, does not participate in the budgeting, does not want to know. The engaged spouse carries the burden and the anxiety alone. The avoiding spouse enjoys the comfort of ignorance. And the power imbalance — because financial control is power, whether or not the controlling spouse intends it to be — grows wider with every year of avoidance.

The Theology of Money in Marriage

The Bible treats money as a diagnostic tool. It does not tell you how much to save or how much to spend. It tells you that your relationship with money reveals your relationship with God. "Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also" (Matthew 6:21). The verse is not a prohibition against having treasure. It is a warning that your treasure — whatever you value most, whatever you protect most fiercely, whatever you worry about losing — will reveal the location of your heart. And in a marriage, the way each spouse relates to money reveals the location of their heart with uncomfortable precision.

The spouse who cannot stop saving is placing their security in the account balance rather than in God. I say this not as judgment but as diagnosis, because I recognize the pattern in myself. The anxiety that drives compulsive saving is the anxiety of a heart that does not trust God to provide. It is the functional atheism of the Israelites who gathered more manna than they needed, despite God's explicit instruction that each day's portion would be sufficient. The extra manna rotted. It always does. Because the security we manufacture for ourselves is not the security God offers. It is the illusion of security, sustained by vigilance and anxiety, and it consumes the very life it was meant to protect.

The spouse who cannot stop spending is placing their identity in acquisition rather than in God. The purchase provides a momentary relief from the emptiness, a brief injection of significance, a temporary sense that life is abundant. But the relief fades, the significance evaporates, and the emptiness returns, demanding another purchase. Ecclesiastes 5:10: "Whoever loves money never has enough; whoever loves wealth is never satisfied with their income." The wisdom is three thousand years old. The pattern has not changed.

Neither saving nor spending is inherently sinful. Both are necessary. The question is what drives them — whether the saving is prudence or fear, whether the spending is generosity or compulsion, whether the money is a tool in service of the marriage or an idol in competition with it.

The Power Dynamics

Money is power in a marriage, and the refusal to acknowledge this truth does not make it less true. It makes it more dangerous, because unacknowledged power operates without accountability.

In marriages where one spouse earns significantly more than the other — or where one spouse earns and the other does not — the earning spouse holds a structural power advantage that shapes every financial decision. The non-earning spouse may technically have equal access to the accounts. They do not have equal standing in the negotiation. The unspoken reality — "I earned this money" — hangs over every conversation about how the money is spent, even when it is never said aloud. Especially when it is never said aloud, because the unspoken has a power that the spoken cannot match.

The stay-at-home parent is particularly vulnerable to this dynamic. Their contribution to the household — the cooking, the cleaning, the child-rearing, the emotional labor that keeps the family functioning — is invisible in the economy's accounting. It does not generate a paycheck. It does not appear on a balance sheet. And in a culture that equates value with earning power, the stay-at-home parent absorbs a subtle but persistent message: your work does not count. This message, absorbed over years, erodes the parent's sense of agency in financial decisions and can produce a dependency that feels less like partnership and more like permission.

The covenant of marriage demands the dismantling of this power dynamic. Not because power differences are inherently sinful but because the covenant transforms two individuals into one economic unit, and the resources of that unit belong to the unit, not to the individual who generated them. Paul's language in 1 Corinthians 7 about the body applies to the finances: "The husband's income does not belong to the husband alone, and the wife's income does not belong to the wife alone." I am paraphrasing, but the principle holds. The one-flesh union does not permit the financial sovereignty of either partner.

The Practice of Financial Unity

What does financial unity look like in practice? It looks like two people sitting at the same table, looking at the same numbers, with equal voice and equal information, making decisions together. This is simple to describe and agonizing to practice, because it requires both spouses to expose their money stories, their fears, their desires, and their shame — and money shame is among the deepest and least discussed shames a person can carry.

The practice begins with full transparency. Both spouses must know the complete financial picture — all income, all debt, all assets, all obligations. The spouse who hides a credit card balance or a savings account or a financial obligation is not protecting the marriage. They are lying to it. And financial deception, while it lacks the dramatic force of sexual infidelity, is a betrayal of the covenant that erodes trust with the same corrosive effect.

The practice continues with regular financial conversations — not the crisis conversation that happens when the credit card bill arrives, but the proactive, scheduled, calm conversation about where the money is going, where it should go, and what each spouse values. These conversations will be uncomfortable. They will expose differences that feel irreconcilable. They will surface the childhood wounds that neither spouse has fully processed. And they are absolutely necessary, because the alternative — financial silence, financial avoidance, financial unilateralism — produces the very outcomes that both spouses fear.

The practice is sustained by a shared vision. What are we building together? What do we want our money to make possible? What would our finances look like if they reflected our actual values rather than our unexamined habits? These questions are not merely financial. They are theological. They ask what the marriage is for, what the family serves, and whether the life being built reflects the kingdom or merely the culture.

Generosity as Marital Practice

I will say one more thing, because it is true even though it sounds counterintuitive: one of the most powerful things a couple can do for their marriage is give money away. Generosity — regular, sacrificial, deliberate giving — does something to a marriage that no budget software can replicate. It breaks the grip of scarcity. It dismantles the idol of security. It forces both spouses to confront the question that every money fight is ultimately about: do we trust God to provide, or do we trust ourselves?

The couples in my congregation who tithe — who give ten percent or more of their income to the church and to the poor — are not wealthier than the couples who do not. But they fight about money less. Not because they have solved the financial puzzle but because generosity has loosened money's hold on their hearts. The money has been put in its place. It is a tool, not a god. And a tool does not generate the anxiety that a god demands.

Every money fight is an invitation — an invitation to go deeper, to name the fear, to excavate the story, to ask what the money actually represents and whether the thing it represents can be found in a balance sheet or only in the God who owns everything and gives freely to those who ask.

The invitation is uncomfortable. It always is. But the couples who accept it — who sit down together and do the hard, humbling work of understanding not just what they earn and spend but why they earn and spend the way they do — those couples discover something that the money itself could never buy: the freedom of two people who are no longer controlled by the thing they thought they were controlling.

I learned this in my own marriage. I grew up without a father, and the absence left me with a money story written in fear — the fear that provision could disappear without warning, the fear that I would not be enough, the fear that the people I loved would go without. I saved compulsively. I budgeted rigidly. I said no to things that would have brought my family joy because the joy cost money and money, in my internal economy, was the only barrier between my family and catastrophe. My wife did not share this fear. She grew up in a household where money was present and shared freely, where generosity was practiced without anxiety, where the future was trusted. She saw my saving as control. I saw her spending as recklessness. We were both wrong. We were both right. And the resolution did not come through compromise — split the difference, save half, spend half. It came through the slow, painful, deeply personal work of telling each other our stories and listening to what the stories revealed.

That freedom is available. It is costly. And it begins not with a better budget but with a braver conversation.

chapters.title: Parenting Through Divorce
chapters.summary: You will want to explain to your children why it was the other parent's fault. Do not. That impulse feels like justice. It is a knife you are handing your child.
chapters.body:
You will want to explain to your children why it was the other parent's fault. Do not. That impulse feels like justice, feels like protecting them from a distorted version of events, feels like the truth they deserve. It is a knife, and you are handing it to your child to carry, and it will cut them for the rest of their lives, not the parent you aimed it at.

I am a pastor. I believe marriage is meant to last, and I do not write this to make divorce comfortable. I write it because divorce happens, it happens in the church, it happens to people who fought for their marriages and to people who did not, and when it happens there are children in the house, and those children did not choose any of it, and how the parents behave in the wreckage will shape those children more than the divorce itself. The divorce is a wound. The way you handle it is either a bandage or salt.

The Thing Children Actually Fear

Ask children of divorce what they were most afraid of, and it is almost never the logistics. It is the fear that it was their fault, and the fear that a parent who left the marriage might leave them too. Children are natural egocentrists, not out of selfishness but out of developmental necessity, and a young child genuinely believes the world revolves around them, which means when the world breaks, they assume they broke it. If I had been better, if I had not fought with my brother, if I had been easier, they would have stayed together.

The child is not asking whose fault the divorce was. The child is asking whether the divorce was their fault. And every argument you win in front of them about the other parent confirms their worst fear, that the family is a war and they are somewhere near the cause.

You have to say it, out loud, more than once, in words a child can hold. This is not your fault. Nothing you did caused this and nothing you could have done would have prevented it. This is between the adults, and both of us still love you, and that is never going to change. You will feel like you are stating the obvious. You are not. The child does not know it. The child needs to hear it from both parents, repeatedly, over years, because the fear is not defeated in one conversation. It comes back at every developmental stage in a new disguise.

The second fear, that a parent who left the marriage might leave the child, is subtler and just as real. A child watches one parent walk away from a relationship they thought was permanent, and the child does the math. If that bond could break, what about mine. This is why divorced parents have to be almost obsessively reliable about the small things, the pickups, the promises, the phone calls, the being where you said you would be when you said you would be there. Every kept promise is evidence against the fear. Every broken one confirms it. The child is running an experiment, mostly unconsciously, on whether the adults in their life can be counted on, and the divorce has already returned one frightening result. Your reliability is how you argue with it.

Do Not Make Them a Messenger

The single most damaging habit in a divorce is turning the child into a courier. Tell your father he still owes for the field trip. Ask your mother why she was late again. Every message you send through the child forces the child to carry your conflict on their small back, across the demilitarized zone, into the other parent's house, where they will absorb the return fire. You have made your child a diplomat in a war they did not start and cannot end.

Children are not messengers. They are not spies, either, though divorced parents interrogate them constantly, what did your mother say, is there a new man there, how much did that cost, framed as concern, functioning as reconnaissance. The child learns to manage information between two hostile powers, to say different things in different houses, to survive by becoming a small deceiver. This is corrosive to the soul of a child. The adults have to communicate with each other, directly, even when it is excruciating, so that the child can just be a child in both houses instead of a courier in neither.

I know how hard the direct communication is, because the whole reason you divorced is often that direct communication became unbearable. But the alternative, routing your conflict through a child, does not spare the child the conflict. It embeds them in it. If you cannot talk to your former spouse without it becoming a fight, then use writing, use a scheduling app, use a mediator, use anything that is not your nine-year-old. The child is not a neutral channel. The child loves both of you, which means every message they carry costs them something in loyalty and every hostility they witness lands on a heart that is already divided in half.

Do Not Recruit Them

There is a deeper betrayal than using a child as a messenger, and it is using a child as a confidant. The lonely, wounded parent who, out of genuine pain, begins to lean on the child emotionally, to share adult grievances, to make the child their support system, their ally, their friend. It feels like closeness. The child even seems to want it, seems mature enough for it, rises to it. It is one of the most damaging things a parent can do.

When you make your child your emotional support, you have not gained an ally. You have lost a child. You have handed them a weight they were never built to carry, and they will carry it, because they love you, and it will bend them.

The child who becomes the parent's confidant loses their childhood. They become anxiously attuned to the adult's emotional state, responsible for a grief they cannot fix, and torn in half when the confided-in grievance is about the other parent they also love. They are being asked to take a side in the destruction of their own family. Some of them do take a side, and it looks like loyalty, and it is really a child being conscripted. Your grief is real and it deserves support. It deserves support from other adults. Your child is not a peer, no matter how mature they seem, and treating them as one steals something from them they do not get back.

This is hardest for the parent who is genuinely alone, whose marriage ended and whose support system thinned out at the same time, and whose most available, most sympathetic listener is the child sitting across the table. I understand the pull. But the pull has to be resisted, precisely because it is so strong and the child is so willing. A twelve-year-old who has become their mother's best friend is not being honored by the closeness. They are being robbed of the freedom to be twelve, to have their own problems be the big problems, to lean on the adult instead of propping the adult up. Find adult support, however hard that is to find, so that your child gets to keep being your child.

Two Houses, One Childhood

The practical work of parenting through divorce is the work of protecting the child's world from becoming a battlefield of contrasts. Two households, run by two hurt people, will differ. But the more the child experiences the two houses as opposed camps with opposed values, the more the child has to fracture themselves to belong in both. Consistency between houses, on the things that matter, bedtimes, expectations, the basic sense of what is right, is a gift to the child's coherence. You are not doing it for your ex. You are doing it so your child does not have to be two different people.

This requires something almost impossible, a working relationship with the person who broke your heart. Not friendship. Not forgiveness on any timeline that can be rushed. A working relationship, businesslike, focused entirely on the child, in which you can sit at the same graduation and the same wedding decades later without the child having to manage your feelings. The parents who achieve this, and some do, give their children something worth more than the intact marriage would have given a different family, proof that love for a child can outlast the love between the adults.

Your Anger Is Real, and It Is Not the Child's to Hold

None of this means your anger is wrong. If you were betrayed, abandoned, or wounded, the anger is righteous and it deserves a place. It deserves a therapist, a pastor, a friend, a journal, the psalms of lament that were written by people who wanted God to break the teeth of their enemies. God can hold your rage. Your congregation can hold your grief. What cannot hold it, what must not be asked to hold it, is a nine-year-old who loves both of the people you are enraged at each other about.

I have sat with divorced parents who were doing everything right in every visible way and were still leaking their bitterness into the child through a thousand small tells, the tone when the other parent's name comes up, the tightness at drop-off, the sigh. Children read these fluently. The work is not to feel nothing. That is impossible. The work is to find adult places for the adult feelings so that the child gets a parent instead of a co-belligerent.

There is a particular temptation that deserves naming, because it is so easy to justify. It is the temptation to let the child see just a little of the truth about the other parent, to plant one small correction, to make sure the child knows, quietly, who was really at fault. It never feels like weaponizing the child. It feels like honesty, like fairness, like refusing to let a lie stand. But the child does not experience it as fairness. The child experiences it as being asked to hold their parent in contempt, and every such request, however small, however justified, tears at the child's own sense of self, because the child is made of both of you. To ask a child to despise one parent is to ask them to despise half of themselves. Whatever the other parent did, and it may have been genuinely terrible, the child's need to love both of you intact is more important than your need to be proven right, and the parent who grasps this, and holds their tongue at the cost of never getting the vindication they crave, is giving the child something worth more than the truth about who broke the marriage.

What Grace Looks Like in the Wreckage

I said I am a pastor and I believe marriage is meant to last. I also believe in grace, and grace is not a doctrine that lives in the abstract, it is a way of behaving toward people who have hurt you. The parent who, in the wreckage of a divorce, refuses to weaponize the children, who honors the other parent in front of them even while grieving privately, who absorbs the messenger role instead of assigning it, who finds adult support instead of conscripting the child, is doing something profoundly Christlike. They are absorbing cost so that someone smaller does not have to. That is the shape of the cross, transposed into custody arrangements and drop-off schedules.

None of this is possible in your own strength, and I will not pretend it is. To honor the person who betrayed you, to hold your tongue when you could win the child to your side, to absorb the messenger role and the loneliness and the rage without leaking any of it onto a child, is genuinely beyond the natural capacity of a wounded human heart. It requires grace poured into you before you can pour it out, the grace of a God who himself absorbed betrayal and did not retaliate, who was wronged past all measure and answered with forgiveness. You will not manufacture this behavior by trying harder. You will only find it by going to the God who did it first and asking him to do it in you, over and over, on the hard mornings, at the drop-offs, in the moments when everything in you wants to make the child understand who the real villain was. The grace you extend to your former spouse for the sake of your children is not something you generate. It is something you receive and pass through, and the passing through is itself the healing, both for you and for the children who are watching.

Your children are watching how you treat the person who hurt you most. They will learn, from that, more about the gospel than from every sermon they hear, because they will see whether grace is real or only spoken. The divorce is not the last word over your children. The way you carry them through it can be a testimony louder than the marriage would ever have been. Not because the divorce was good. It was not. But because grace does its best work exactly where things have broken, and your children are old enough to see, in you, whether you believe that or only preach it. Show them. It is the most important sermon you will ever give, and you will give it without words, in the years when it costs the most.

chapters.title: Protecting Your Marriage From the Demands of Work
chapters.summary: Work does not steal your marriage by being evil, it steals it by being good, by giving you the clear scoreboard and visible reward that marriage withholds, until you are quietly more married to the job.
chapters.body:
A man told me, with no apparent grief, that his marriage had become a logistics partnership. He and his wife coordinated children and calendars and money with great efficiency, and they had not had a real conversation in months, and he reported this the way you would report the weather, because nothing dramatic had gone wrong. No affair. No fight. The marriage had simply been crowded out, one good and urgent work demand at a time, until what remained was a smooth-running operation with two strangers at the controls. He had not chosen against his wife on any single day. He had chosen against her on a thousand days so small that none of them felt like a choice.

This is how work takes a marriage, and the reason it is hard to fight is that work does not present itself as the enemy. The affair is obvious. You can repent of an affair. But how do you repent of being responsible. How do you name the problem when the problem is that you provided, that you answered the email, that you took the meeting, that you did the thing everyone praised you for doing. Work does not seduce a marriage by being a vice. It seduces by being a virtue, and a virtue is much harder to resist than a vice, because you feel righteous the whole time you are losing the thing that matters most.

Let me give the strongest version of the counterargument, because there is one and it is not stupid. The objection says that providing for your family is itself an act of love, that the man or woman grinding at a demanding job is not neglecting the marriage but serving it, building the security and the future the family depends on, and that the soft talk about presence and connection is a luxury belief held by people who have never worried about rent. Work is how you love them, the objection says. The paycheck is the affection in usable form. And there is real truth in that, enough that I will not wave it away. Provision is love. The parent working a double shift to keep the lights on is not failing the family, they are carrying it, and any pastor who lectures that parent about quality time has never been poor and should sit down.

Where the objection fails is in the slide it permits, the slide from work is a way of loving them to work is the way of loving them, and from there to a place where the providing has entirely replaced the presence and the provider tells himself the replacement is the gift. The man in my office was not poor. His extra hours were not keeping the lights on. They were buying a slightly larger house and a great deal of esteem, and he had wrapped the whole thing in the language of provision because provision is the respectable name for it. The honest provision the objection defends and the quiet abandonment I am describing can look identical from outside, and the difference is whether the work is serving the marriage or has become the rival the marriage now serves. Most of us cannot tell which we are doing, because the same activity hosts both, and we always narrate ourselves as the provider and never as the deserter.

Let me carry one text. In the second creation account, before any work goes wrong, God puts the man in the garden to work it and keep it (Genesis 2:15 ESV), and then immediately declares that it is not good for the man to be alone and makes the woman, and the order matters. Work comes first in the text and the marriage comes second, but the marriage is the thing declared not good to be without. Work is given as a vocation and it is genuinely good. The one flesh is given as the answer to a lack that work could not fill, because the man in the garden was already working and still alone, and his aloneness was not solved by more garden. Here is the diagnostic the text hands us. If you are working harder and lonelier, you are repeating the man's pre-marriage condition inside your marriage, surrounded by good labor and still unaccompanied, and no amount of additional good labor will touch it, because labor was never the cure for aloneness. It was the context the cure was given into.
