The contest I am describing is not timeless, though it feels that way, and naming when it sharpened helps. For most of human history work and marriage occupied the same ground. The household was the workplace, the farm and the shop were where the couple labored side by side, and there was no commute between the two because there was no distance to cross. The Industrial Revolution of the nineteenth century pried them apart, pulling work out of the home and into the factory and the office, and once work happened somewhere the marriage could not see, the two became rivals for the same hours instead of partners in the same labor. The man who told me his marriage was a logistics partnership is living in the architecture that separation built. He leaves the marriage every morning to go to the place where work is, and the leaving is so normal that he never notices he is choosing one location over the other, every day, by reflex. The scoreboard I am about to describe got its power from that arrangement, because once the work moved out of sight, it was the only one of the two that came home with a number attached.

The reason work wins, practically, is that it offers what marriage by its nature withholds. Work gives you a scoreboard. There are deadlines met, numbers hit, projects shipped, promotions granted, a steady stream of visible evidence that you are competent and that you matter. Marriage offers no such scoreboard. The work of marriage is mostly invisible, rarely rewarded in any legible way, and never finished. So when a person is starving for the feeling of competence, and most of us are, work feeds them and marriage does not, and they drift toward the thing that feeds them, and they call the drift ambition. The cruelest part is that the better you are at your work, the stronger the pull, because the rewards are richer and the scoreboard lights up brighter, and the marriage, which never lights up at all, recedes by comparison until it is a logistics partnership and you did not even feel it go.

So the protection of a marriage from work is not finally about time management, though it involves time. It is about correctly identifying what is happening, which is a contest between two things competing for the center of your life, one of which announces its claims loudly with deadlines and one of which makes its claims silently and loses every loud contest by default. The marriage will never out-shout the job. It cannot. It does not have the volume. Which means the only way it survives is if you decide, in advance and against the noise, that it sits at the center and the work serves it, and then you defend that decision on the small days when nothing seems to be at stake, because the small days are the only days there ever are.

What does the defense look like, concretely. It looks, first, like protected unproductive time, hours given to the marriage that produce nothing and prove nothing, where you are not solving a logistics problem together but simply present to each other with no scoreboard running. This will feel like a waste to a person trained by work, and the feeling that it is a waste is precisely the disease. The most important time in a marriage is time that accomplishes nothing measurable, and a person who can only justify time by its output has already been colonized by the logic of the job, and the marriage is dying of efficiency.

It looks, second, like a hard limit you set when no crisis demands it, a place where the work is told no on principle and not on emergency. The man who waits for a work demand extreme enough to justify refusing it will never refuse anything, because the demands are individually always reasonable. You stop the encroachment by drawing the line in calm weather, by deciding that this evening, this day, this season is not available to the job, and holding it when the job comes asking politely with a request that is, taken alone, entirely fair. The fairness of each individual request is the mechanism of the loss. You defeat it only by refusing on grounds that precede the request.

It looks, third, like telling the truth about what your work is actually buying, because the provision story is sometimes true and sometimes a cover, and only you and God know which. Eugene Peterson spent his life warning pastors that busyness is not a sign of devotion but a sign of disordered loves, that the busy person is usually busy because being busy is the way they avoid the harder and quieter work of actually being present to the people in front of them (Peterson 1989). His warning was to pastors but it indicts all of us. Ask whether your hours are feeding your family or feeding your need to feel important, and refuse the easy answer, because the easy answer is always provision and the true answer is sometimes vanity wearing provision's coat.

Here is the reversal. We protect our marriages from work as though the threat were that work will take our time, and time is part of it, but the deeper theft is that work will reshape what we think a person is for. Spend enough years in a world that measures you by output and rewards you by results, and you will start, without deciding to, treating your spouse as a project to be managed rather than a person to be known, applying to the marriage the only logic you have left, the logic of efficiency and return. The man with the logistics partnership had not just given his hours to the job. He had given the job his imagination, and it had taught him to see his wife as a coordination problem, and that deformation of his seeing was the real damage, deeper than any missed dinner.

The cross does the work, and the law comes first, severe and exact. Genesis put the marriage at the center as the answer to aloneness and you have let a good thing climb up and take that center, and you cannot serve two masters, and the master you actually serve is the one you reorganize your real life around, not the one you praise on Sunday. By that measure many of us are married to our work and merely cohabiting with our spouse, and the law says so plainly and gives no relief. But the grace is that the God who put the man in the garden to work it is the same God who declared his aloneness not good and gave him another, and that God does not ask you to abandon your work to save your marriage. He asks you to put it back in its place, under the marriage and not over it, and the One who orders all loves rightly is willing to reorder yours, beginning the moment you stop calling the disorder provision and name it for what it is.

The man left and did not change overnight, because no one does, and the marriage that erodes over a thousand small days is rebuilt the same way, a thousand small days back. But he started by admitting that the logistics partnership was not the accidental residue of responsibility. It was the predictable result of a contest he had been losing for years without knowing a contest was on. Work did not steal his marriage by being bad. It stole it by being good, and by being loud, and by being where the scoreboard was, and he had wandered toward the lights like everyone does. The marriage was still there, quiet in the dark where he had left it, waiting to be chosen on a day when nothing forced the choice. That is the only kind of day there is. Choose it then, or you will not choose it at all.

### Works Cited

Peterson, Eugene H. The Contemplative Pastor. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1989.

The Holy Bible, English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

chapters.title: Second Marriages: Grace, Baggage, and Starting Again
chapters.summary: The second marriage carries everything the first marriage taught — including things both spouses wish they had not learned. Grace does not erase the past. It makes the past usable.
chapters.body:
The second wedding is different from the first. Not necessarily smaller or less festive, though it often is both. Different in texture. The vows land differently in a mouth that has spoken them before. The promise to love until death do us part carries a different weight when you know, from experience, that the part can come long before death. The guests clap and smile, and some of them are thinking what the couple is thinking but will not say: we hope this one works.

Second marriages are the church's most awkward category. We do not quite know what to do with them. We believe in the permanence of marriage, and here are two people whose first marriages were not permanent. We believe in new beginnings, and here is a beginning that is not entirely new — it is built on the foundation of something that ended, and the ending is part of the structure whether we acknowledge it or not. We believe in grace, but we are not sure how far grace extends. Does it extend to a second chance at the thing you failed at the first time? Does it extend to happiness after the covenant was broken? Does grace have a statute of limitations?

It does not. But the church has often acted as though it does, and second marriages have paid the price.

What the Second Spouse Inherits

The person who marries someone with a previous marriage inherits more than a partner. They inherit a history — a history that includes wounds they did not inflict, patterns they did not create, and sensitivities they will trip over in the dark for years before they learn where they are.

The previously married spouse carries reflexes from the first marriage. If the first marriage ended because of criticism, they will flinch at anything that sounds like criticism in the second. If the first marriage ended because of emotional withdrawal, they will panic at any sign of distance. If the first marriage ended because of infidelity, they will scan for threats with a vigilance that feels, to the new spouse, like mistrust. And it is mistrust — not of the new spouse, but of marriage itself. The first marriage taught them that marriage can fail, and they carry that knowledge into the second marriage like a scar that aches before rain.

The second spouse did not cause these reflexes. They did not earn this mistrust. But they must live with it, and the living-with-it requires a patience that nobody warns them about. "I am not your ex" is the sentence that every second spouse eventually says, and it is true and it is necessary and it does not solve the problem, because the problem is not rational. It is somatic. It lives in the body, in the nervous system, in the place where the first marriage wrote its lessons in a language the conscious mind cannot always read.

The Baggage Everyone Mentions and Nobody Defines

People speak of "baggage" in second marriages the way they speak of "issues" in therapy — vaguely, as if the word itself explains something. It does not. Baggage, in the context of second marriage, means specific things, and naming them is the beginning of dealing with them.

Financial baggage: the debt from the first marriage, the alimony or child support payments, the lifestyle adjustment that comes with dividing one household into two. The second marriage starts with less than the first marriage had, and the disparity between expectation and reality can generate resentment before the honeymoon is over.

Relational baggage: the ex-spouse who is still in the picture because children require co-parenting, the in-laws from the first marriage who are now the grandparents of the new spouse's stepchildren, the friendships that were forged during the first marriage and may not survive the transition to the second. The second marriage does not begin with a clean relational slate. It begins in the middle of a relational web that was already in place.

Emotional baggage: the grief of the first marriage's failure, the guilt (whether warranted or not) about the role one played in that failure, the fear that history will repeat itself, the defensive patterns developed during the worst of the first marriage that now get deployed in the best of the second. The second spouse reaches for their partner's hand and the partner pulls away — not because they do not want to be touched, but because the last person who reached for their hand used touch as a prelude to a fight.

The church cannot remove this baggage. But it can stop pretending it does not exist. The pastoral preparation for a second marriage should differ substantially from the preparation for a first marriage — not because second marriages are less holy, but because they face different challenges. The couple entering a second marriage needs to name their baggage explicitly, to each other and to their community, and they need a community that can hold that naming without judgment.

The Ghost of the First Marriage

Every second marriage has a ghost. The ghost is the first marriage — not the ex-spouse as a person, but the first marriage as a template, a reference point, an invisible standard against which the second marriage is constantly measured.

The measurement works in both directions. Sometimes the second marriage is measured favorably: "He never listened to me the way you do." "She was never this affectionate." These comparisons feel like compliments, but they are not. They are reminders that the new spouse exists in relation to the old one, that their virtues are defined not on their own terms but in contrast to someone else's failures. No one wants to be loved as the correction of a previous mistake.

Sometimes the measurement works unfavorably, and this is worse. "My first husband always remembered my birthday." "My first wife kept a cleaner house." These comparisons, even when unspoken, create an impossible standard — a standard defined by selective memory, because the first marriage is now remembered not as it was but as it is wished it had been. The dead marriage, like the dead in general, gets idealized. Its faults fade. Its virtues sharpen. And the living spouse — the one who is present, imperfect, doing their best — cannot compete with a memory.

The second marriage must exorcise this ghost, and the exorcism is simple to describe and difficult to execute: stop comparing. Not "stop saying it out loud." Stop doing it. This requires a discipline of the mind that borders on spiritual practice — the deliberate choice, repeated hundreds of times, to judge the current marriage on its own terms rather than against the template of the previous one. It is the decision to let this marriage be this marriage, with its own shape, its own rhythms, its own particular combination of strengths and weaknesses that has never existed before and will never exist again.

Grace and the Second Chance

The theological question at the heart of the second marriage is whether grace extends to second chances — and if so, what that grace looks like. The church has historically been ambivalent about this, and the ambivalence shows in the way we treat second marriages: we perform them, but with less enthusiasm. We celebrate them, but with a footnote. We welcome them, but we wonder, privately, whether God blesses what God did not originally intend.

This ambivalence is understandable. It is also unnecessary. The entire narrative of Scripture is a story of second chances — of God who makes covenant, watches the covenant broken, grieves the breaking, and makes covenant again. Abraham lied about Sarah. Twice. God renewed the covenant. David committed adultery and murder. God did not abandon the Davidic line. Peter denied Jesus three times. Jesus restored him three times. The pattern is relentless: human beings break things, and God, instead of writing them off, offers them another chance to build something faithful.

If this is the pattern of God's dealing with humanity, then the church must stop treating the second marriage as a concession and start treating it as an instance of the pattern. Grace does not erase the past — the first marriage happened, the failure happened, the pain happened, and none of it is undone by the second ceremony. What grace does is make the past usable. It transforms the failure from a disqualification into a teacher. It says: what you learned in the fire, bring it into this new thing. Let the scars inform the love. Let the grief deepen the gratitude. Let the failure make you humble enough to succeed.

What the Second Marriage Needs from the Church

The second marriage needs the church to do four things.

First, welcome without asterisk. The couple entering a second marriage does not need to be reminded that their first marriage failed. They know. They carry it every day. What they need is a community that receives them as they are — with their history, their children, their complications — and says, "You are home here."

Second, pastoral care that acknowledges the complexity. Second marriages face challenges that first marriages do not: blended family dynamics, co-parenting with ex-spouses, the integration of different family cultures, the management of financial obligations from previous relationships. The church that applies its standard first-marriage counseling to a second marriage is not being efficient. It is being lazy.

Third, patience with the timeline. Second marriages take longer to reach their stride. The couple is not just learning each other — they are learning each other while unlearning the patterns of a previous relationship. This takes time. More time than the church usually offers before it starts asking, "How are things going?" with that particular pastoral inflection that means, "Are you sure this was a good idea?"

Fourth, the freedom to grieve. The second marriage does not erase the grief of the first marriage's ending. That grief will surface — at unexpected times, triggered by unexpected things — and the second spouse must be allowed to feel it without the new partner interpreting it as a commentary on their relationship. The person who grieves their first marriage while building their second is not being unfaithful to the second. They are being human. And the church must make room for the grief alongside the new beginning.

The second marriage is an act of courage that the church does not always recognize as such. It is the decision to try again — knowing what failure costs, knowing what the odds are, knowing that the scars of the first attempt will ache in weather they cannot predict. It is the most human thing in the world: to be broken and to choose, despite the brokenness, to love again.

The God who makes all things new does not require that the old things never happened. God requires only that we bring them — all of them, the joy and the wreckage — and lay them down, and begin.

chapters.title: Servant Leadership vs. Domination
chapters.summary: The word headship has been used to justify a kind of control the Scriptures never endorse. The biblical picture is not softer than the world's leadership. It is more costly, because the leader dies first.
chapters.body:
Few biblical ideas have been more abused than the notion of male leadership in the home, and I want to handle it with the seriousness the abuse demands. On one side, the word headship has been used to justify control, dismissiveness, and in the worst cases outright cruelty, a man ruling his household like a small kingdom and quoting Scripture to sanctify it. On the other side, the reaction against that abuse has led many to throw out the biblical language entirely as inherently oppressive. I think both are mistakes, and I think the actual biblical picture, when we finally look at it, is more radical and more costly than either the abusers or the critics have understood.

The word we skip over

When Paul writes to husbands about their role, there is a word we tend to skip over in our rush to the part about the wife, and skipping it is how the whole thing gets twisted. The husband is told to love his wife as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her. That phrase, gave himself up, is the entire definition of the headship being described, and it is almost the exact opposite of what domination assumes.

Christ's love for the church is defined by a single act, the cross, in which he did not exercise power over her but laid his life down for her. The model for the husband, then, is not a king on a throne issuing commands, but a savior on a cross bleeding for the beloved. The headship of the husband is a headship defined by self sacrifice, by dying, by being the one who bears the greatest cost. Any use of the word headship that does not begin and end with the husband's death for his wife has severed the word from its only meaning and made it into its opposite.

Biblical headship is not the right to be served. It is the obligation to die first. The head is the one on the cross.

How the world defines a leader

To feel the radicalism of this, set it against how the world understands leadership, and how the fallen male heart naturally understands it. In the world's picture, the leader is the one at the top, the one whose will prevails, the one others exist to serve, the one who benefits from his position. Leadership means being served. It means your comfort is prioritized, your preferences carry, your voice is decisive. The leader is the one who gets and the followers are the ones who give.

This is the picture the dominating husband is working from, whether he knows it or not, and he has simply added a religious justification to it. He believes headship means his will should prevail, his comfort should be served, his preferences should organize the home, and his wife and children exist in some sense to support his position. He may be sincere. He may believe he is doing exactly what the Bible commands. But he has poured the world's definition of leadership into the biblical word and completely inverted its meaning, because the biblical word was pointing at the cross the whole time, and the cross is the death of the world's definition.

How Jesus redefined it on purpose

Jesus did not leave this to inference. He confronted the world's model of leadership directly and overturned it deliberately, and he did it in response to his own disciples jockeying for position. When they argued about who would be greatest, he told them that the rulers of the world lord it over people and call it greatness, but it shall not be so among you. Whoever wants to be great must be the servant, and whoever wants to be first must be the slave of all, for even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and to give his life as a ransom.

Read that carefully, because it is a direct assault on the entire concept of domination, spoken by the one person who had every right to dominate. He does not say leadership is bad. He says leadership among his people runs in the exact opposite direction from leadership in the world. The world's leader is served. The kingdom's leader serves. The world's leader is first and benefits most. The kingdom's leader is last and pays most. And Jesus roots this not in a rule but in his own example, the one with all authority washing feet and going to a cross, so that no follower of his could ever again baptize domination and call it leadership.

It shall not be so among you. Four words that ban forever the leadership that lords it over others, spoken by the only one who had the right to.

What servant leadership actually costs

Here is what I most want the man who resists this to understand. Servant leadership is not the soft, weak, abdicating thing that dominating men fear it is. It is not a husband who has no spine, who never decides anything, who lets his family drift because leading feels too much like domination. That is not servant leadership, that is abdication, and it is its own failure. The servant leader genuinely leads. He takes responsibility, he bears weight, he makes hard decisions, he watches the horizon, he goes first into difficulty.

The difference is not whether he leads but for whom and at what cost. The dominating leader leads for himself and makes others pay. The servant leader leads for the good of those he serves and pays the cost himself. When there is sacrifice to be made, the servant leader makes it. When there is a hard and thankless task, he takes it. When someone must go without, it is him. When there is fear to be carried, he carries it so his family does not have to. This is not less leadership than domination. It is far more, because it is far harder, and it costs the leader everything rather than costing the followers everything.

The dominating man, in truth, is taking the easy path and calling it leadership. It is easy to make your will prevail when you hold the power. It is easy to be served. What is hard, unspeakably hard, is to hold real authority and to spend all of it on the good of others, to lead by going lowest, to be the head by being the one on the cross. The world has never called that leadership, but it is the only leadership the Scriptures recognize, and it is the only kind a Christian man is permitted.

Authority that produces flourishing

One more thing must be said, because there is a way of hearing all this that leads a man to conclude authority itself is suspect, that any exercise of leadership in the home is a step toward domination, and that the safest thing is to hold no authority at all. That is the abdication we already named, and it is not the answer. The servant leader does hold real authority. The question is what his authority is for.

Consider how the best kind of authority actually works, even in the created order. A trellis holds up a vine so that the vine can flourish and bear fruit it could never bear collapsed on the ground. The trellis is not dominating the vine. Its structure exists entirely for the vine's flourishing. This is the shape of servant authority. The husband and father who leads well provides a structure within which the people he loves can flourish, can feel safe, can grow into who God made them to be. His authority is not aimed at his own comfort or his own will. It is aimed at their flourishing, and it is measured by their flourishing, and if the people under a man's leadership are shrinking, fearful, diminished, then whatever he is exercising, it is not the servant authority the Scriptures describe.

So the goal is not the absence of authority but the redemption of it. A home needs a man who will bear responsibility, who will make hard decisions, who will provide the steady structure within which a family can rest and grow. What it does not need is a man who confuses that responsibility with the right to be served, who treats his authority as a possession to be enjoyed rather than a burden to be borne for others. The difference between a trellis and a cage is not the presence of structure. Both have structure. The difference is whether the structure exists for the flourishing of what it holds or for the will of the one who built it. Servant leadership builds trellises. Domination builds cages. And a man's family always knows, in their bodies, which one they are living inside.

How a wife knows the difference

There is a simple way to tell whether a man's leadership is servant leadership or domination, and it does not depend on the man's own assessment, because dominating men almost always believe they are serving. The test is in the effect on the people led. Ask the wife of a servant leader what it is like to live under his leadership, and she will describe safety, rest, the sense of being cherished and protected, the freedom to be herself, the experience of a man whose strength is spent on her good. Ask the wife of a dominating man the same question, and she will describe fear, walking on eggshells, the constant management of his moods, the sense of being an instrument of his will rather than a person he serves.

Both men may use the same language. Both may quote the same verses about headship. But the fruit is opposite, and the fruit does not lie. A woman living under servant leadership flourishes, expands, becomes more fully herself, because that is what the leadership is for. A woman living under domination shrinks, dims, becomes a smaller version of herself, because the leadership is bent toward the man's will rather than her flourishing. If a man wants to know which kind of leader he actually is, he should not consult his own intentions, which will flatter him, but the state of the people he leads, which will tell him the truth.

A dominating man almost always believes he is serving. The truth is not in his intentions but in whether the people he leads are flourishing or shrinking.

It is worth being clear about what this means for the ordinary decisions of a home, because the abstraction can float away from daily life. Servant leadership does not mean a man has no voice or that every decision is endlessly negotiated until no one leads at all. It means that when the man's voice carries weight, that weight is spent on the good of the household rather than the satisfaction of his preferences, and that his default posture is to prefer his family's flourishing over his own comfort. When there is a genuine impasse and someone must finally decide, the servant leader does decide, and bears the responsibility for the decision, but he decides as one accountable to God for the good of those he leads, not as one exercising a right to get his way. The authority is real. Its whole orientation is simply the reverse of domination.

The servant leader, for his part, welcomes this test rather than fearing it, because he actually wants to know the truth about his effect on the people he loves. He asks his wife how his leadership feels to her, and he means it, and he is willing to hear a hard answer without retaliating, because his goal is her flourishing and not the protection of his own self image. The dominating man cannot do this, because he cannot bear to be told he is dominating, and his inability to receive the feedback is itself a symptom of the very problem. A man who genuinely wants to serve will seek out the honest assessment of the served. A man who wants to be right will avoid it, and the avoidance tells the truth he is unwilling to hear.

This is a frightening test, because it takes the assessment out of the man's own hands, where he could keep it comfortable, and puts it in the observable reality of his home. But it is a mercy, because it gives a man an honest mirror. If those under his care are fearful, guarded, diminished, then whatever he tells himself, he is dominating, and the language of biblical headship he has draped over it is a covering for the very thing the Scriptures forbid. And if they are flourishing, safe, expanding into who God made them to be, then his authority, however imperfect, is being spent the way Christ spent his, on the good of the beloved rather than the will of the self.

I have to examine my own leadership by this measure, and it does not always pass. It is easy, in a home and in a church, to slide toward the leadership that serves myself, that prioritizes my comfort, that makes others carry what I should carry, and to dress it up in the language of authority and headship and calling. The question that keeps me honest is the one Jesus's redefinition forces on every man who would lead. Am I leading for them or for me. Am I the one paying the cost or the one collecting the benefit. Am I on the cross or on the throne. The answer, when I am honest, sends me back to the only pattern that has any right to the word, the head who washed feet, the King who died, the leader who was great because he made himself the servant of all.

chapters.title: Sexual Intimacy as Theology
chapters.summary: The church has managed to make sex both an idol and a taboo simultaneously — but Scripture treats sexual intimacy as a theological act, a bodily enactment of the covenant that reveals something about God that nothing else can.
chapters.body:
The church has a sex problem, and the problem is not what most people think. It is not that the church talks about sex too much or too little. It is that the church talks about sex badly — vacillating between two equally distorted positions. The first position treats sex as danger, something to be fenced off, warned against, and guarded from with purity pledges and metaphors about chewed gum and used tape. The second position, the evangelical reaction to the first, treats sex as reward — God's gift to married people, the prize for doing it right, the holy pleasure that makes all the waiting worthwhile. Both positions reduce sex to something it is not. Neither arrives at what it is.

What sex is, in the biblical framework, is theology. Not a metaphor for theology. Not an illustration of theological principles. An actual theological act — a bodily enactment of the covenant, a physical participation in the mystery that Paul says is "profound," a revelation of something about God and humanity that cannot be accessed any other way. The church that cannot say this clearly — that cannot hold together the goodness, the gravity, and the vulnerability of sexual intimacy without collapsing into either prudishness or banality — has failed at one of its most fundamental pastoral tasks.

I write this as a pastor who has sat with hundreds of couples whose sexual lives are sources of pain, shame, confusion, and grief. I write this as a man who grew up in a culture that saturated him with sexual imagery and a church that gave him almost nothing to counter it except rules. I write this knowing that the subject requires more honesty than the church typically permits and more reverence than the culture typically offers. Both are necessary. Neither alone is sufficient.

The Body Is Not the Problem

The deepest distortion in the church's theology of sex is the assumption, rarely stated but pervasively felt, that the body is the problem. That the sexual urge is a concession to fallen nature rather than a feature of created goodness. That the spiritual life is the real life and the bodily life is the obstacle to it.

This assumption does not come from the Bible. It comes from Plato, filtered through Gnosticism, absorbed by certain strands of early Christianity, and embedded so deeply in Western religious consciousness that most Christians do not realize they hold it. The Gnostic heresy taught that the material world was created by a lesser deity, that the body was a prison for the soul, and that salvation consisted in escaping the body's demands. The early church condemned Gnosticism formally. It absorbed Gnosticism practically. And the practical absorption shows up most clearly in the church's treatment of sex.

The biblical witness is unambiguous. "God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good" (Genesis 1:31). Everything. The bodies. The hormones. The desire. The capacity for physical pleasure. All of it preceded the fall. All of it was pronounced good before sin entered the picture. The Song of Solomon — an entire book of erotic poetry that the church has spent centuries trying to allegorize into something safer — celebrates the beauty of the human body and the pleasure of sexual desire with an explicitness that would make most church small groups deeply uncomfortable.

"Your lips drip nectar, my bride; honey and milk are under your tongue" (Song 4:11). "Let my beloved come to his garden, and eat its choicest fruits" (Song 4:16). "I came to my garden, my sister, my bride, I gathered my myrrh with my spice, I ate my honeycomb with my honey" (Song 5:1). The language is sensual. It is deliberate. And it is Scripture. The God who inspired these words is not embarrassed by the body. The question is why we are.

Origen of Alexandria, one of the early church's greatest minds, castrated himself in response to Matthew 19:12 — a literalism so extreme that even the church of his day condemned it. But the impulse behind Origen's act — the conviction that the body's desires are the enemy of the soul's purity — survived his censure and infected Christian theology for centuries. Augustine, whose own sexual history shaped his theology in ways he did not fully acknowledge, treated concupiscence as the mechanism through which original sin was transmitted. The implication was devastating: the sexual act, even within marriage, was tainted by the fall. It was permitted, but it was not clean. The stain of that theology is still on the church's hands.

The One-Flesh Union Revisited

I have written elsewhere about the meaning of "one flesh" in Hebrew, and I will not repeat that analysis in full here. But the sexual dimension of the one-flesh union requires specific attention, because it is the dimension the church most consistently mishandles.

When two bodies come together in sexual union, something happens that is not merely biological. The act of sexual intercourse is the most complete physical vulnerability two human beings can share — the removal of every barrier, the exposure of every surface, the mutual surrender of bodily autonomy. It is the bodily enactment of what the covenant promises verbally: I am yours. All of me. Without reservation. Without defense.

This is why sexual intimacy outside of covenant — outside the binding, permanent, public commitment — is, in the biblical framework, not merely rule-breaking but self-contradictory. The body is saying what the will has not said. The act of total physical surrender is being performed without the context of total personal commitment. The flesh is becoming one while the lives remain separate. And the resulting dissonance — the gap between what the body says and what the life says — is what the biblical writers call porneia, sexual immorality. Not because the body is bad. Because the body is saying something that is not true.

Within the covenant, sexual intimacy becomes something else entirely. It becomes a sacramental act — a visible, physical sign of an invisible, spiritual reality. The mutual self-giving of two bodies mirrors the mutual self-giving of two lives. The pleasure is not the point, though it is genuinely good. The vulnerability is the point. The willingness to be fully exposed, fully received, fully held by another person who has promised not to leave — this is what makes marital sex a theological act rather than merely a physical one.

The Damage Done by Purity Culture

I cannot write about sexual intimacy in marriage without addressing the wreckage left by the purity culture movement of the 1990s and 2000s. The movement — epitomized by Joshua Harris's "I Kissed Dating Goodbye" (1997), the True Love Waits campaign, and a thousand youth group talks featuring crumpled roses and unwrapped candy bars — was built on a legitimate concern: young people were being harmed by the sexual chaos of the culture, and the church wanted to protect them.

But the protection was purchased at a catastrophic price. Purity culture taught, implicitly and often explicitly, that sexual desire was the enemy — that the body's longing for intimacy was something to be suppressed, controlled, and feared. It taught women that their bodies were dangerous — sources of temptation that must be hidden, covered, and guarded lest they cause a brother to stumble. It taught men that their desire was predatory — an animal impulse that, if not caged by accountability partners and internet filters, would destroy everything it touched.

The result was a generation of Christians who arrived at their wedding nights carrying not anticipation but terror. Sheila Wray Gregoire's research, published in "The Great Sex Rescue," documented what many pastors had observed anecdotally: women who had absorbed purity culture messaging reported significantly higher rates of sexual pain, difficulty with arousal, and inability to experience pleasure in marriage. The message that sex was dangerous before the wedding did not magically transform into the message that sex was beautiful after it. The body does not work that way. The shame that was learned in adolescence did not evaporate with the exchange of rings. It followed them into the marriage bed and took up permanent residence.

Harris himself eventually renounced both the book and his faith — a trajectory that should give the church pause. When the architect of a movement walks away from the building, it is worth asking whether the foundation was sound. The foundation was not sound. It was built on fear, not theology. On shame, not Scripture. On the premise that the body is the problem, which is the oldest heresy in the Christian tradition, repackaged for the youth group.

The church owes these women — and these men — a profound apology. Not merely for the excesses of the movement but for the underlying theology that made the excesses possible: the theology that treats the body as the enemy of the soul, that confuses purity with repression, that cannot distinguish between sexual discipline and sexual fear.

What Healthy Sexual Theology Requires

A theology of sexual intimacy adequate to the biblical witness must hold together at least four things that the church has historically separated.

First, it must hold together goodness and gravity. Sex is good — genuinely, bodily, pleasurably good. It is also weighty — a covenantal act with the power to bond, to heal, to wound, and to reveal. A theology that has only goodness produces triviality. A theology that has only gravity produces fear. The biblical witness holds both: the Song of Solomon's delight and Paul's warning that the body is a temple. The pleasure and the weight belong together. Separating them distorts both.

Second, it must hold together desire and discipline. Sexual desire is not the enemy. It is a created capacity, a gift of the God who made bodies and pronounced them good. But desire, like every created capacity, requires direction. The discipline is not the suppression of desire but the training of desire — learning to want what is good, in the way that is good, at the time that is good. This is true of every appetite. The solution to gluttony is not the elimination of hunger. It is the ordering of hunger toward its proper end. The same is true of sexual desire.

Third, it must hold together mutuality and difference. Paul's instructions in 1 Corinthians 7 are striking in their symmetry: "The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband. For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does." The symmetry is deliberate and radical. In a first-century context where a wife's body was legally the property of her husband, Paul insists that the authority is mutual. Both bodies belong to the other. Both partners have the right to give and the obligation to receive. Neither can claim ownership without reciprocating it.

This mutuality has been badly abused. The passage has been used to coerce unwilling spouses into sex — "your body is not your own" deployed as a weapon rather than an invitation. This is a perversion of Paul's meaning so profound that it constitutes its own form of sexual sin. The mutuality Paul describes is not about obligation. It is about generosity — the willingness of two people to give themselves to each other freely, without coercion, without manipulation, and without the withholding of the self as punishment.

Fourth, and most difficult, it must hold together the sexual and the sacred without making them identical. Sex is not worship. It is not a substitute for prayer. It does not earn spiritual credit. But it participates in something sacred — the covenant between two people that mirrors the covenant between God and humanity. The church that cannot make this distinction will either sacralize sex into something oppressively holy or desacralize it into something casually biological. Both errors miss the point.

The Practical Realities

Theology that does not touch the ground is not theology. It is abstraction. And the ground where sexual intimacy lives in most marriages is more complicated than any theological framework can fully address.

There are couples in every congregation dealing with mismatched desire — one partner who wants sex frequently and another who does not. There are couples dealing with sexual dysfunction — pain, inability to achieve arousal or orgasm, erectile difficulty — that makes the physical act of union difficult or impossible. There are couples carrying wounds from sexual abuse — one in four women and one in six men, according to the CDC — whose bodies respond to sexual touch with fear rather than pleasure. There are couples who have never had an honest conversation about what they enjoy, what they need, and what they do not want, because the church gave them a theology of sex that was too embarrassed to get specific.

These realities require more than theology. They require clinical competence, professional counseling, medical intervention, and the kind of pastoral care that is willing to sit in uncomfortable specificity rather than retreating to comfortable abstraction. The pastor who cannot refer a couple to a sex therapist without embarrassment is not protecting the sanctity of the subject. That pastor is failing the people who need help.

The body is not the enemy of the soul. It is the place where the soul lives. And the sexual union of two people within the covenant of marriage is not a concession to human weakness. It is a participation in divine self-giving — the bodily enactment of a love that holds nothing back, that refuses to hide, and that trusts the other with the whole unguarded self.

The church that can say this — can say it without blushing, without hedging, without retreating into either prudishness or crudeness — will be a church that finally gives its people what they need: not rules about sex, but a theology of sex. A theology that honors the body, respects the covenant, takes pleasure seriously, and refuses to let shame have the last word about something God called very good.

I have watched couples in my congregation discover, sometimes after decades of marriage, that they had never talked honestly about sex. Not once. They had done it. They had avoided it. They had fought about it. They had endured it. But they had never talked about it — about what they wanted, what they feared, what they enjoyed, what they needed. The silence was not because they were private people. It was because the church had given them no language for the conversation. The only language available was the language of rules — what is permitted, what is prohibited — and rules do not cover the terrain that matters most. The terrain that matters most is the terrain of two embodied souls trying to be fully present to each other in the most vulnerable act available to human beings. That terrain requires a language of reverence, curiosity, honesty, and grace. The church has barely begun to develop it.

That theology is overdue. The people in our pews have been waiting for it. Some of them have stopped waiting. The church that speaks last speaks to an empty room.

chapters.title: Submission Revisited: What Ephesians 5 Actually Says
chapters.summary: Ephesians 5 has been used to silence women and empower men for centuries. A serious reading of the text reveals something far more radical — and far more costly — than either side of the debate wants to admit.
chapters.body:
No passage of Scripture has been more weaponized in the history of marriage than Ephesians 5:22-33. "Wives, submit to your husbands as to the Lord." Those eleven words have been quoted to justify everything from benign patriarchy to outright abuse, from the gentle insistence that the husband should make the final decision to the violent demand that the wife should obey without question. They have been embroidered on pillows, preached from pulpits, and whispered by abusers to their victims as theological justification for cruelty.

And they have been quoted, almost always, out of context. Torn from the passage that surrounds them, stripped of the revolutionary framework in which Paul placed them, and deployed as a proof text for a power arrangement that the passage itself subverts.

It is time to read the text again. Not the eleven words. The whole passage. And not with the assumptions that two thousand years of patriarchal interpretation have layered onto it, but with the eyes of someone encountering Paul's argument for the first time, in the context in which it was written, to the audience that first received it.

What we will find is not what either the complementarians or the egalitarians expect. What we will find is harder, more beautiful, and more costly than either camp has been willing to say.

The Verse They Always Skip

The passage does not begin at verse 22. It begins at verse 21: "Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ." This verse is the heading — the thesis statement — of everything that follows. Paul's instruction to wives does not emerge from a vacuum. It emerges from a prior, overarching command to mutual submission. Every relationship that Paul addresses in the following verses — wives and husbands, children and parents, slaves and masters — is nested under this controlling statement: submit to one another.

This matters enormously. If verse 22 is read in isolation, it establishes a one-directional hierarchy: wives submit to husbands. But if verse 22 is read as a specific application of verse 21, the hierarchy is reframed. The wife's submission is one expression of a mutual submission that characterizes the entire Christian community. The husband is not exempted from submission. He is included in it by the verse that governs the passage.

The church has, for most of its history, read verse 22 without verse 21. This is not an accident. It is a choice — a choice made by interpreters who benefited from the hierarchical reading and who had every incentive to ignore the verse that complicated it. When you begin at verse 22, you get patriarchy. When you begin at verse 21, you get something else entirely. You get a community in which power is not exercised over others but surrendered for others. You get a marriage in which both spouses are called to the same fundamental posture: submission — not to each other's authority, but to each other's good.

What "Submit" Actually Means

The Greek word translated "submit" is hupotasso. In its military usage, it means to arrange oneself under — to place oneself in a position of subordination within an ordered structure. But Paul is not writing a military manual. He is writing to a community that has been turned upside down by the gospel, in which the first are last and the last are first, in which the greatest is the servant of all. In this context, hupotasso does not mean "obey a superior." It means "orient yourself toward the good of another person, even at cost to yourself."

This is a crucial distinction. Obedience is compelled by authority. Submission, in Paul's usage, is offered by love. It is not the response of an inferior to a superior. It is the response of a free person who chooses, voluntarily, to prioritize another's well-being. It is what Jesus modeled in the foot-washing — the one with all the authority choosing to serve the one with none. The submission Paul calls for is not the submission of weakness. It is the submission of strength voluntarily restrained for the sake of love.

The wife who submits in this sense is not diminishing herself. She is orienting herself — toward her husband's good, toward the good of the marriage, toward the pattern of Christ who submitted himself to death for the sake of those he loved. This is not a demeaning posture. It is the most exalted posture the New Testament knows.

But — and this is where the complementarian reading goes wrong — it is not a posture required only of wives.

What the Husband Is Actually Told

Paul's instruction to husbands occupies three times the space of his instruction to wives. This is not an accident. In a first-century context, the wife's submission was assumed. It was the cultural default. The husband's authority was unquestioned. Paul did not need to spend time establishing what everyone already accepted. What he needed to establish — what required argument, what was genuinely radical — was the limitation and redefinition of that authority.

"Husbands, love your wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her." This is not a general instruction to be nice. It is a specific instruction to die. The model Paul holds up is not Christ the King, not Christ the Ruler, not Christ the Head who exercises power over the body. It is Christ the Crucified — the one who emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and was obedient unto death. The husband's love is to look like that.

In a first-century household — in a world where the husband had near-absolute legal authority over his wife, where he could divorce her at will, where he owned her property and controlled her social access — this instruction was not a reinforcement of the status quo. It was its demolition. Paul tells the husband: your authority is real, and it exists for one purpose only — to be spent on behalf of your wife. You do not exercise it over her. You exercise it for her. You do not use your position to get what you want. You use your position to give what she needs. And if the giving costs you everything — if it costs you your comfort, your preferences, your very life — that is precisely the cost Christ paid, and it is the cost you signed up for when you entered this covenant.

The husband who reads Ephesians 5 and concludes that he is in charge has read three verses and missed the other nine. He has seen his authority and missed its purpose. He has claimed the throne and ignored the cross that stands behind it.

The Head-Body Metaphor

Paul says the husband is the "head" of the wife as Christ is the head of the church. The word "head" — kephale in Greek — has generated more scholarly debate than perhaps any other word in the Pauline corpus. Does it mean "authority over," as the complementarian tradition insists? Or does it mean "source," as some egalitarian scholars have argued?

The honest answer is that the debate is not settled, and both sides have legitimate arguments. But what is more important than the precise meaning of kephale is the model Paul attaches to it. Whatever "head" means, it means what Christ's headship means. And Christ's headship, as Paul describes it in this passage, means giving himself up — not exercising authority over the church, but sacrificing himself for the church's good.

If "head" means "authority," then the authority is self-sacrificial. If "head" means "source," then the source is self-giving. Either way, the husband's role is defined not by what he gets from the relationship but by what he gives to it. The head that does not serve the body is not a head in any Christian sense. It is a tumor.

This is not what the complementarian tradition has typically taught. The typical complementarian teaching says: the husband leads, the wife follows. The husband decides, the wife submits. The husband is the head, the wife is the body. These formulations, while they sound like Ephesians 5, actually reverse the passage's logic. The passage does not say the husband leads and the wife follows. It says both submit — the wife through willing orientation toward her husband's good, the husband through self-sacrificial love that takes Christ's death as its model. Both postures are forms of submission. Neither is a claim to power.

What the Passage Does Not Say

Ephesians 5 does not say the husband makes the decisions. It does not say the wife must obey. It does not say the husband has the final word. It does not say the wife cannot lead, teach, earn, think, or speak. It does not say the husband's opinion carries more weight. It does not establish a chain of command. It does not create a hierarchy of value, worth, intelligence, or spiritual capacity.

These are things the church has read into the passage — projecting the patriarchal assumptions of its culture onto a text that was, in its original context, far more subversive than the church has been willing to recognize. First-century wives did not need to be told to submit; the culture already required it. What was revolutionary was the instruction to husbands — the limitation of their authority, the redefinition of their headship, the insistence that their power existed solely for the purpose of self-sacrificial love.

The tragedy of the church's use of Ephesians 5 is that it has taken a passage that originally limited the husband's power and used it to expand it. It has taken a passage that originally elevated the wife's dignity and used it to diminish it. It has turned a revolutionary text into a reactionary one — and in doing so, it has done violence to the text, to women, and to the marriages that the text was meant to serve.

What Mutual Submission Looks Like

If Ephesians 5 is read as Paul intended — beginning at verse 21, with mutual submission as the controlling principle — what does it produce? Not the complementarian hierarchy. Not the egalitarian erasure of all difference. Something harder and more beautiful than either.

It produces a marriage in which both spouses are constantly asking: what does love require me to give up? Not what does love entitle me to. What does love require me to surrender? This is the question that the cross asks every relationship, and it is the question that mutual submission embeds in the daily life of the marriage.

Sometimes love requires the wife to defer to her husband — not because he has authority over her, but because his judgment is sound and her deference serves the good of the family. Sometimes love requires the husband to defer to his wife — not because she has authority over him, but because her wisdom exceeds his and his deference serves the good of the family. The direction of deference is not fixed by gender. It is determined by wisdom, by context, by the specific needs of the specific moment. And both spouses are willing to defer, because both spouses have internalized the same principle: I am here to serve, not to be served.

This is harder than hierarchy. Hierarchy is simple: someone is in charge, someone is not. Mutual submission is complex: both are in charge, both are not, and the negotiation of who leads in which moment requires a level of maturity, trust, and communication that hierarchy does not demand. But the difficulty is the point. Marriage is supposed to be a crucible — a context in which both people are shaped into the image of Christ. And the shape of Christ is not the shape of authority. It is the shape of a cross.

The Cost of Getting This Wrong

The church's misreading of Ephesians 5 has had consequences that cannot be measured. Women who were told that God required their submission to men who were harming them. Men who were told that their authority was divinely sanctioned and therefore beyond question. Marriages in which one person's voice was elevated and the other's was silenced — not by mutual agreement, but by a theological framework that was presented as biblical and was, in fact, a cultural projection onto a text that said something else entirely.

I have sat with the women who were damaged by this misreading. I have heard their stories. I have watched them struggle to disentangle the God they were taught from the God who actually exists — the God who does not require their diminishment, who does not sanction their suffering, who does not use the language of love to enforce the reality of control.

And I have sat with the men who were damaged by it too — men who were told they were the leaders and discovered, to their bewilderment, that the crown was heavy and the authority was isolating and the marriage they were supposed to lead was dying because their wife did not need a leader. She needed a partner. She needed a friend. She needed someone who would submit to her — to her needs, her wisdom, her experience, her voice — the way she had been told, all her life, to submit to him.

Ephesians 5 is one of the most beautiful passages in Scripture. It envisions a marriage in which both people pour themselves out for each other, in which authority is exercised as service, in which the pattern of Christ's self-giving love becomes the pattern of daily life. The church has turned it into a hierarchy. It is time to turn it back.

The cross is not a throne. And the marriage that is built on the cross is not built on power. It is built on the willingness to lay power down.

chapters.title: The Emotionally Absent Spouse
chapters.summary: The most common complaint in my office is not about affairs or addiction — it is about the spouse who is physically present and emotionally gone, and the loneliness of lying next to someone who is not really there.
chapters.body:
The complaint arrives in my office in different words, but it is always the same complaint. "He is there but he is not there." "She has shut down and I cannot reach her." "We live in the same house and I have never been lonelier." The presenting issue varies — sometimes it is framed as a communication problem, sometimes as a conflict about parenting or money or sex. But underneath the presenting issue, the wound is the same: one spouse has become emotionally absent, and the other is starving.

Emotional absence is not dramatic. It does not announce itself with a crisis or a revelation. It is quiet, gradual, almost invisible. The absent spouse still comes home. They still eat dinner at the table. They still sleep in the same bed. They may even be pleasant, competent, responsible. They pay the bills, mow the lawn, drive the kids to practice. From the outside, nothing is wrong. From the inside, everything is wrong, because the one thing that makes a marriage a marriage — the emotional connection between two people — has been withdrawn.

This is the most common and least discussed form of marital suffering. It does not make the headlines like infidelity. It does not trigger the alarm bells like addiction. It is a slow starvation — a death by inches — and the person experiencing it often cannot explain what is wrong because nothing identifiable has happened. The spouse has not done anything wrong. That is precisely the problem. They have not done anything at all.

What Emotional Absence Looks Like

Emotional absence manifests in patterns that are recognizable once you know what to look for. The absent spouse does not initiate conversation about anything beyond logistics. They do not ask how your day was and mean it. They do not notice when you are upset. They do not respond when you try to share something that matters to you — a worry about the children, a frustration at work, a moment of beauty that you wanted to share. They are not hostile. They are not cold, exactly. They are simply elsewhere — their attention directed inward or outward, anywhere but at you.

The absent spouse often does not realize they are absent. This is not an excuse. It is a diagnostic observation. Many emotionally absent people are not withholding intentionally. They are living inside a pattern they did not choose and cannot see — a pattern formed in childhood, reinforced by culture, and sustained by the sheer momentum of adult life. They learned early that the safest place to be was inside themselves, that emotional exposure was dangerous, that the best way to survive was to become a fortress. The fortress kept them safe as children. It is killing their marriage as adults.

The absent spouse may also be absent because they are overwhelmed. The demands of work, parenting, financial pressure, and the constant low-grade anxiety of modern life can consume the emotional resources that the marriage needs. The spouse who comes home after a twelve-hour workday, having managed people and problems and crises for someone else's profit, may simply have nothing left. The tank is empty. And the marriage, which requires fuel to run, stalls. This form of absence is not a character flaw. It is a structural problem — a problem of a culture that extracts more from its workers than human beings were designed to give.

The attachment literature is helpful here. John Bowlby, the British psychiatrist who developed attachment theory in the mid-twentieth century, identified a pattern he called "avoidant attachment" — a relational style formed in early childhood when the primary caregiver was consistently unavailable or unresponsive. The child learns that emotional needs will not be met, and rather than continuing to reach out into empty space, the child adapts. The child learns to suppress the need, to self-soothe rather than seek comfort, to build an internal world that does not depend on anyone else.

This adaptation is brilliant in childhood. It is a survival strategy of remarkable sophistication. And it is catastrophic in adulthood, because the strategy that was designed to protect the child from the pain of unmet attachment needs now prevents the adult from meeting their spouse's attachment needs. The avoidant partner is not choosing to be distant. They are running software written thirty years ago, in a context that no longer exists, for a purpose that no longer applies.

The Pursuing Spouse's Dilemma

The spouse on the other side of emotional absence faces a dilemma that has no easy resolution. They need connection. They are married to someone who does not provide it. And every strategy they employ to get it tends to make the problem worse.

The most common strategy is pursuit — escalating attempts to draw the absent spouse out. More questions. More requests for conversation. More expressions of need. More complaints about the distance. The pursuit is logical: if the problem is distance, the solution should be closeness. But in the attachment dynamic, pursuit triggers withdrawal. The absent spouse, already overwhelmed by the demand for emotional engagement they do not know how to provide, retreats further. The pursuing spouse, interpreting the retreat as rejection, pursues harder. The cycle accelerates until both are exhausted — the pursuer angry and depleted, the withdrawer cornered and shut down.

Sue Johnson, the developer of Emotionally Focused Therapy, calls this the "pursue-withdraw cycle" and identifies it as the single most common pattern in distressed couples. The pattern is not a character flaw in either partner. It is a system — an interlocking set of behaviors that each partner triggers in the other, sustained by the attachment fears that both carry. The pursuer fears abandonment. The withdrawer fears engulfment. Both fears are real. Both are driving the behavior that makes the other's fear come true.

The cruelest dimension of this cycle is that both partners are in pain. The pursuing spouse's pain is visible — the tears, the anger, the desperate attempts to connect. The absent spouse's pain is invisible — the shame, the paralysis, the terrible awareness that they are failing at the one relationship that matters most and have no idea how to stop failing. The pursuing spouse sees a partner who does not care. The absent spouse sees a partner who can never be satisfied. Both are wrong. Both are suffering.

The Gendered Dimension

I need to say something about gender here, because the research consistently shows a gendered pattern in emotional absence, and ignoring the pattern does not serve the couples who live inside it.

Men are disproportionately the emotionally absent partner. Not exclusively — women can be emotionally absent, and the experience is equally painful when they are. But the pattern skews male, and the reasons are not mysterious. Boys in Western culture are systematically trained out of emotional expression from an early age. "Boys don't cry." "Man up." "Don't be so sensitive." The socialization is relentless, and by adulthood, many men have lost access to their own emotional interior — not because the emotions are not there, but because the capacity to identify, name, and express them has atrophied from disuse.

Niobe Way's longitudinal research, published in "Deep Secrets," documented that adolescent boys in the United States have rich, emotionally intimate friendships in early adolescence that they systematically abandon by late adolescence, under the pressure of masculine norms that equate emotional closeness between males with weakness or homosexuality. By adulthood, the average American man has zero intimate friendships — zero people to whom he can say what he actually feels. His wife is often the only person in his life with whom emotional intimacy is even theoretically possible. And he has been trained, for his entire life, to be incapable of it.

This is not an excuse for emotional absence. It is a context. And the church, which has largely reinforced the masculine norms that produce emotional absence — the strong, silent leader, the provider who does not need, the man who leads his family with quiet authority rather than emotional vulnerability — bears a particular responsibility for addressing it.

What the Absent Spouse Must Learn

The emotionally absent spouse must learn something they were never taught: that emotional presence is a skill, not a personality trait, and that skills can be acquired. This learning is painful, because it requires the absent spouse to re-enter the emotional terrain they spent their childhood learning to avoid. It requires them to feel things they have been suppressing for decades. It requires them to be bad at something in front of the person whose opinion matters most.

The learning begins with awareness — the recognition that the absence is real, that it has consequences, and that the spouse's complaints about it are not nagging but a legitimate cry of pain. This recognition is often the hardest step, because the absent spouse's defensive system is designed to minimize the significance of emotional connection. "I am here, aren't I?" "I work hard to provide for this family." "What more do you want?" These responses are not malicious. They are the sound of a defensive system protecting itself from a demand it does not know how to meet.

The learning continues with practice — small, deliberate acts of emotional engagement that, over time, begin to rewire the patterns. Asking a question and waiting for the answer. Noticing when your spouse is upset and saying so. Sharing something you feel — not something you think, but something you feel — without being prompted. Putting the phone down during conversation. Making eye contact. These are elementary things. For the emotionally absent spouse, they feel like crossing a minefield.

The learning is sustained by therapeutic support. I cannot say this strongly enough: the pattern of emotional absence is rarely broken without professional help. The defensive system that produces the absence is deeply embedded, often rooted in childhood experiences that the absent spouse has never processed. A competent therapist — particularly one trained in emotionally focused therapy or attachment-based approaches — can guide the absent spouse into the emotional territory they have been avoiding, with the safety and structure that makes the re-entry survivable.

What the Pursuing Spouse Must Learn

The pursuing spouse's learning is equally difficult, though it takes a different form. The pursuer must learn to regulate their own anxiety without depending on the absent spouse's response. This does not mean suppressing the need for connection. It means finding ways to soothe the attachment fear that drives the pursuit — developing the internal resources that allow them to tolerate the gap between what they need and what their spouse can currently provide.

The pursuer must also learn to translate their anger into vulnerability. The absent spouse does not respond to anger. Anger triggers their defensive system and drives them further into withdrawal. But vulnerability — the soft, exposed expression of the need beneath the anger — can sometimes reach the absent spouse in a way that anger cannot. "I miss you" lands differently than "You never talk to me." "I am scared we are losing each other" lands differently than "You do not care about this marriage." The message is the same. The delivery determines whether it is received.

This is not fair. I know it is not fair. The pursuing spouse should not have to translate their legitimate pain into a form the absent spouse can receive. But fairness and effectiveness are not the same thing, and the goal is not to win the argument but to reach the person. And reaching the person sometimes requires speaking their language rather than demanding that they learn yours.

What the Church Must Do

The church must stop celebrating emotional absence as spiritual maturity. The quiet, steady, unemotional man is not the model of Christian masculinity. He may be the victim of a socialization process that has cut him off from half of his own humanity. The church that holds up stoicism as a virtue is holding up a wound as a trophy, and the marriages in its pews are paying the price.

The church must create spaces where emotional honesty is possible — where men can say what they actually feel without being judged, where vulnerability is treated as strength rather than weakness, where the pastoral leadership models emotional presence rather than emotional performance. This requires pastors who are themselves willing to be emotionally present — not performed vulnerability for a sermon illustration, but genuine, risky, unscripted honesty about their own inner lives.

The emotionally absent spouse is not a villain. They are a person who learned, long before they learned to love, that the safest place in the world was inside themselves. The work of marriage — and the work of the Spirit — is to show them that there is a safer place: the space between two people who have chosen to stay, to feel, and to be fully present to each other, not because it is natural but because it is necessary, and not because it is easy but because it is love.

That work is long. It is humbling. It does not produce the dramatic breakthroughs that make for good testimonies. It produces small, incremental changes — a question asked, an emotion named, a hand held in silence — that accumulate over years into something that begins to resemble the intimacy both partners have been craving.

I have watched this happen in my own marriage. I have been the emotionally absent spouse — present in body, absent in soul, giving the church everything and giving home the remnants. I have sat across from my wife and realized, with a shame I cannot adequately describe, that she was telling me something important and I had not heard a word. Not because I was not listening. Because I had nothing left to listen with. The empathy had been spent on parishioners. The attentiveness had been deployed in counseling sessions. The capacity for emotional presence had been distributed across forty hours of pastoral work, and the well was dry.

The recovery was not dramatic. It was not a single conversation or a breakthrough moment. It was a slow, humbling relearning of skills I should never have let atrophy — the skill of asking a question and caring about the answer, the skill of putting the phone down without being asked, the skill of noticing the look on my wife's face and saying, "Something is wrong. Tell me." These are elementary skills. I had to learn them like a child learning to walk. And the relearning required a willingness to be bad at something in front of the person whose judgment I feared most. That willingness, more than any technique or insight, was the beginning of the return.

The intimacy will not look like the movies. It will look like two imperfect people, fumbling toward each other in the dark, learning to say the things they were never taught to say. It will be awkward and halting and sometimes painful. It will also be real. And real, in a marriage, is worth more than any performance could ever be.

chapters.title: The Empty Nest Marriage
chapters.summary: The day the last child leaves is the day the marriage discovers whether it was a partnership or a parenting arrangement — and for many couples, the silence that fills the house is the loudest thing they have ever heard.
chapters.body:
The house gets quiet. It does not get quiet gradually, the way the mornings lengthen in spring. It gets quiet all at once — a door closing, a car pulling out of the driveway, a bedroom that is suddenly just a room. The child who filled that room — who filled it with noise and mess and need and presence — is gone. Not gone permanently, not gone irretrievably, but gone in the way that matters for the daily life of the household. The dinner table has an empty chair. The bathroom counter has space. The schedule, which for two decades was organized around someone else's needs, is suddenly and disoriently organized around nothing.

And the two people who remain — the couple who built this life, who raised these children, who spent twenty or twenty-five or thirty years in the consuming project of parenthood — look at each other across the quiet house and realize that they are, in some essential sense, strangers. Not hostile strangers. Not indifferent strangers. But strangers in the way that two people become strangers when they have spent decades standing side by side, facing the same direction, attending to the same tasks, without ever turning to face each other.

The empty nest is not a vacation. It is a reckoning. And the marriage that has not prepared for it — that has used the children as the connective tissue between two people who stopped connecting with each other years ago — will find the reckoning devastating.

The Statistics and the Silence

The divorce rate among adults over fifty has doubled since 1990, according to research by Susan Brown and I-Fen Lin at Bowling Green State University. The phenomenon is significant enough to have earned its own label: "gray divorce." And while gray divorce has multiple causes — longer lifespans, reduced stigma, financial independence of women, the influence of the baby boom generation's cultural values — one of the most common precipitating factors is the departure of the last child.

The AARP survey on divorce after fifty found that 66 percent of divorces in this age group were initiated by women. The most commonly cited reason was not infidelity or abuse. It was emotional disconnection — the sense of having grown apart, of living with someone who no longer knew them, of enduring a marriage that was functional but dead. The women who left did not leave in anger. Many left in grief — grief for the marriage they had wanted, grief for the intimacy they had never received, grief for the years they had spent waiting for the relationship to become what it had never been.

The men, by and large, were blindsided. They thought the marriage was fine. They had been providing, protecting, working, doing the things they understood marriage to require. The fact that their wives were starving — emotionally, conversationally, romantically — did not register, because the language of emotional starvation was not in their vocabulary. They were not bad men. They were men who had mistaken presence for connection and provision for partnership, and the mistake, uncorrected across decades, proved fatal.

I pastor men in this exact situation. I have watched the bewilderment on their faces when they discover, in their fifties, that the wife they thought was content was actually enduring. The bewilderment is genuine. They did not know.
