They did not know because they did not ask, and they did not ask because the culture that shaped them did not teach them that asking was part of the job description. The failure is real. The responsibility is theirs. But the context matters, because understanding how we got here is the first step toward getting somewhere else.

What the Children Were Covering

The departure of the children does not create the distance between spouses. It reveals it. The distance was always there, hidden beneath the noise and activity of family life. The children provided a shared project, a common purpose, a daily structure that made the marriage feel active even when the marriage itself was dormant. You do not need to connect with your spouse when every evening is consumed by homework supervision, sports practice transportation, bedtime routines, and the logistics of managing multiple small lives. The children filled the space. The children generated the conversation. The children provided the excuse not to face each other.

I do not say this to blame the children. The children did not ask to be the marriage's connective tissue. They did not volunteer to be the buffer between two people who had stopped doing the work of intimacy. They simply filled the available space, because that is what children do. And when they left, the space they had filled revealed what had been there all along: two people who had forgotten how to be married to each other.

This is a particular grief — the grief of discovering, in your fifties or sixties, that the marriage you thought you had was actually a parenting partnership that has now concluded its primary project. The love is not gone. The history is not meaningless. But the relationship, stripped of its organizing principle, feels hollow. And the hollowness is terrifying, because it suggests that the best years of the marriage were not really about the marriage at all.

The Identity Crisis

The empty nest triggers an identity crisis in both spouses, and the crisis is sharper for the spouse whose identity was most fully invested in the parenting role. For many women — particularly those who stayed home during the parenting years or who organized their professional lives around the children's needs — the departure of the last child is an existential event. The role that gave shape to their days, purpose to their decisions, and meaning to their sacrifices has ended. They are still alive, still married, still capable. But they do not know who they are outside the identity of "Mom."

Men face a parallel crisis, though it typically manifests differently. The father who defined himself by his ability to provide and protect discovers that there is no one left who needs his provision or protection in the immediate, daily sense. The house is secure. The college fund is depleted. The work that once felt meaningful — providing for a family — now feels purposeless. What are you working for when the people you were working for have gone?

Both crises are real. Both require attention. And both can either drive the spouses apart — each retreating into their own existential reckoning — or draw them together, if the couple has the courage to face the reckoning as a shared experience rather than parallel solitudes.

The crisis is compounded by the culture's obsession with youth. A culture that worships the young implicitly devalues the old, and the empty-nest couple stands at the threshold of a stage of life that the culture has almost nothing positive to say about. The advertisements do not feature them. The churches do not program for them. The marriage books are written for the newly married or the struggling married, not for the long-married who are trying to figure out what comes next. The cultural silence communicates a message that the empty-nest couple absorbs without realizing it: your best years are behind you. The message is a lie, but it is a pervasive and persuasive one, and the couple that believes it will not invest in a future they do not think they have.

The Opportunity

Here is what no one tells you about the empty nest: it is not only a crisis. It is also an opportunity — the first genuine opportunity in decades for the marriage to become what it was always meant to be. The children are gone. The schedule is open. The energy that was consumed by parenting is available for other investments. The question is what you will invest it in.

The marriages that thrive in the empty nest are marriages that treat the transition not as a loss but as a second beginning. Not a return to the pre-children marriage — that marriage was inhabited by younger, less experienced, less scarred versions of both spouses. A new beginning. A marriage between the people you are now — people who have been shaped by decades of shared experience, who have survived crises together, who carry a depth of history that no new relationship can replicate.

The depth of history is an asset, though it may not feel like one. You know this person. You know their weaknesses and their fears. You know the sounds they make when they sleep. You know how they handle grief and what makes them laugh and what they look like when they are pretending to be fine. This knowledge is not the enemy of romance. It is the foundation of the deepest intimacy available to human beings — the intimacy of being fully known and choosing to stay.

I have watched couples in this stage discover things about each other that they somehow missed during the parenting years. The husband who discovers that his wife has been reading philosophy in the early mornings for years and has thoughts about human consciousness that he never knew about. The wife who discovers that her husband has been quietly grieving his own father's death for a decade and never said a word, because the children's needs always seemed more urgent than his own. These discoveries are both wonderful and devastating — wonderful because they reveal a depth in the other person that the busyness had obscured, devastating because they expose the years of disconnection that allowed the depth to remain hidden.

The empty nest invites you to redeploy this knowledge. To stop knowing each other as co-parents and start knowing each other as companions. To have the conversations you postponed because the children needed dinner. To take the trip you deferred because the schedule would not allow it. To sit on the porch in the evening and discover that the quiet, which felt so threatening at first, is actually the space in which the marriage can finally breathe.

The Work of Reconnection

Reconnection does not happen automatically. It requires the same kind of intentionality that built the marriage in the first place — the willingness to pursue, to be curious, to risk vulnerability, to say things that have gone unsaid for too long.

Start by asking questions you stopped asking years ago. What are you thinking about these days? What do you want the next ten years to look like? What have you always wanted to do that we never did? What are you afraid of? What do you need from me that you have not been getting? These are dangerous questions. They may produce answers you did not expect. They may surface grievances that have been buried for decades. They may reveal desires that feel impossible to reconcile with the life you have built. Ask them anyway. The alternative — the polite, surface-level coexistence of two people sharing a house and a tax return — is not a marriage. It is a roommate arrangement with legal standing.

Reconnection also requires physical reengagement. Many empty-nest couples have let the physical dimension of the marriage atrophy — not necessarily sex, though that may have declined as well, but the entire spectrum of physical connection. Touch. Proximity. The willingness to sit close on the couch rather than in separate recliners. The willingness to reach for each other in bed rather than turning away. The body remembers what the mind has forgotten, and the reintroduction of physical closeness can awaken emotional connections that words alone cannot reach.

Reconnection may require professional help. There is no shame in this. A marriage therapist is not a sign of failure. It is a sign of investment — the decision that this marriage is worth the same kind of professional attention that you would give to your health, your career, or your finances. The couples who seek help early in the empty-nest transition — before the distance calcifies into permanent disconnection — have the best outcomes. The couples who wait until the distance is total and the resentment is established face a much harder road.

The Theological Invitation

The empty nest is a theological moment. It is the moment when the marriage is stripped to its essence — two people, a covenant, and the God who made it. The accessories are gone. The distractions have departed. What remains is the question that every marriage must eventually answer: was this a covenant or a convenience?

If it was a covenant, then the empty nest is not the end of the marriage's purpose. It is the beginning of a new chapter — a chapter in which the purpose of the marriage is no longer the raising of children but the mutual sanctification of two people who have committed to walk together until death. The children were a stewardship, temporary and precious. The marriage is a covenant, permanent and foundational. The stewardship has ended. The covenant continues.

And the covenant, freed from the demands of the stewardship, has the space to become something it could not become while the children were present — something deeper, quieter, more honest, more tender. The love that survives the empty nest is not the love of the honeymoon. It is a love that has been tested by decades of shared life, refined by conflict and forgiveness and the accumulated weight of ten thousand ordinary days. It is a love that does not need to prove itself because it has already been proven — in the staying, in the choosing, in the daily decision to turn toward each other rather than away.

The church has a role to play here — a role it has largely neglected. Most churches invest heavily in premarital counseling and young-married ministry and parenting programs. Almost none invest in empty-nest ministry — in supporting couples through the transition, in creating community for people whose social lives were built around their children's activities, in addressing the specific spiritual and relational needs of people in the second half of life. This is a failure of pastoral imagination, and the gray divorce statistics are, in part, its consequence.

The empty nest is not a void. It is a clearing — a space where two people, freed from the beautiful burden of raising the next generation, can finally turn to face each other and discover whether the love they promised at the altar has survived the years it took to keep the promise.

For many couples, the discovery will be painful. The distance will be real. The work of reconnection will be difficult. But the discovery is also an invitation — an invitation to build something new on the foundation of something old, to let the marriage become what it was always meant to be, to choose each other one more time in the quiet house where the echoes of children's voices are fading and the sound of two people learning to be married again is just beginning.

The beginning is available. It does not require youth or energy or the absence of scars. It requires only the willingness to start — to look at the person across the table and say, not with the passion of the wedding day but with the gravity of someone who knows exactly what the words cost: I am still here. And I want to know you again.

chapters.title: The Five-Year Marriage Check: An Honest Assessment
chapters.summary: Five years into a marriage, the adrenaline of the beginning has faded and the shape of what you are actually building becomes visible. This is the moment to look honestly at what you have made.
chapters.body:
Five years is not a milestone the culture celebrates. There are no special names for a fifth anniversary — no silver, no gold, no diamond. Hallmark makes a card for it, but the card does not know what to say, because five years is an awkward interval: too long to be new, too short to be tested, too ordinary to merit the kind of reflection that longer marriages receive.

But five years is exactly when the reflection is most needed. Because five years is when the marriage you actually have begins to diverge from the marriage you imagined, and the gap between the two — the gap between what you thought this would be and what it is — is either a source of grief or a source of growth, depending on whether you have the courage to look at it honestly.

I have performed enough weddings and counseled enough couples to know that the first two years are consumed by adjustment — by the shock of sharing a bathroom, a budget, a bed with another person whose habits were formed in a different household. Years three and four are consumed by whatever comes next — often a child, sometimes a career change, occasionally a crisis that forces the couple to discover what they are made of before they were ready to find out. But year five — year five is when the dust settles. The patterns are established. The routines are set. The way you fight, the way you make up, the way you spend Saturday mornings — all of it has calcified into a shape. And the question year five asks is: is this a shape you can live in?

The Questions Nobody Asks

The five-year marriage check begins with questions, and the questions must be honest enough to produce honest answers. Not "Are you happy?" — happiness is too vague, too subject to the weather of any given Tuesday, to be a useful diagnostic. The questions must be more specific, more pointed, more willing to cut through the comfortable fictions that five years of shared life inevitably generate.

Do you like this person? Not love — like. Love is a commitment. Like is a preference. You can love someone you do not like, and many five-year marriages are doing exactly that — maintaining the commitment while losing the preference. Do you enjoy their company? Do you look forward to seeing them at the end of the day? Would you choose them again — not in the romantic, cinematic sense, but in the practical sense: if you met them today, knowing what you know, would you want to build a life with this person?

Do you trust this person? Not with the big things — most people trust their spouse not to clean out the bank account or disappear with the children. With the small things. Do you trust them with your feelings? With your failures? With the parts of yourself that you do not show anyone else? Is this person safe? Not safe in the sense of boring. Safe in the sense of: I can be my full self here, including the parts that are weak and foolish and afraid, and I will not be punished for it.

Do you fight well? Not "do you fight" — every couple fights, and the couple that does not fight is a couple that has stopped caring enough to disagree. The question is whether the fighting produces resolution or resentment. Do your arguments end with understanding, even if they do not end with agreement? Or do they end with someone winning and someone losing, with the loser filing the loss away in the growing archive of grievances that will eventually become too heavy to carry?

Are you growing — individually and together? The person you married five years ago is not the person you are married to now. People change. The question is whether you are changing in directions that bring you closer together or further apart. Are your interests diverging? Your values? Your vision of what a good life looks like? Some divergence is natural and healthy. But if the divergence is so great that you cannot find common ground — if you are becoming strangers who share an address — the five-year mark is the time to name it.

The Patterns That Have Set

By year five, the marriage has developed patterns that feel permanent — and that feel permanent because, without intervention, they are. The patterns of communication, conflict, intimacy, and daily life that characterize a five-year marriage are, with minor variations, the patterns that will characterize a fifteen-year marriage and a thirty-year marriage. The couple that does not fight fair at five will not fight fair at twenty. The couple that avoids hard conversations at five will avoid them at fifteen. The couple that has stopped having sex at five will not spontaneously resume at ten.

This is not fatalism. It is observation, supported by decades of marital research. Patterns, once established, have inertia. They persist not because the couple chooses them but because changing them requires more energy than maintaining them. The couple that wants to change a destructive pattern at year five has time and plasticity on their side. The couple that waits until year fifteen has less of both.

The five-year check is, therefore, an opportunity — perhaps the best opportunity the marriage will ever have — to identify the patterns that are not working and to change them before they harden into permanence. This requires honesty that most couples find uncomfortable. It requires saying, "This thing we do — this way we fight, this way we avoid, this way we coexist without connecting — this is not working, and if we do not change it, it will define us."

That sentence is hard to speak. But it is infinitely easier to speak at year five than at year twenty, when the pattern has been reinforced by fifteen additional years of repetition and the prospect of change feels not just difficult but impossible.

The Myth of Effortless Marriage

The five-year mark is often the point at which the couple confronts one of the church's most damaging myths: that a good marriage is an effortless marriage. The myth says: if you married the right person, and if you are both walking with God, the marriage should be natural, easy, a source of joy rather than work. And when the marriage is not easy — when it requires effort, negotiation, compromise, and the daily decision to choose patience over frustration — the myth whispers: something is wrong. You married the wrong person. God is not in this marriage. A good marriage would not be this hard.

This is a lie. Every good marriage is hard. It is hard because it requires two selfish people — and all people are selfish, at bottom, no matter how sanctified — to share a life in which their selfishness is constantly confronted, constantly challenged, constantly required to yield to the needs and desires of another person. This is not a sign that the marriage is failing. It is a sign that the marriage is doing what marriage is supposed to do: sanctifying the people in it. And sanctification is never comfortable.

The couple that reaches year five and finds their marriage difficult has not failed. They have arrived at the real marriage — the one that exists after the honeymoon fades and the infatuation wears off and the person across the table is revealed as a human being with morning breath and bad habits and a capacity for annoyance that the dating period mercifully concealed.

The real marriage is better than the imagined one. Not easier. Better. Because the real marriage is the place where actual love — not the feeling, but the practice — happens. The feeling of love is a gift. The practice of love is a discipline. And the five-year marriage is the place where the discipline either takes root or is abandoned in favor of the fantasy that somewhere, with someone else, the feeling would have lasted.

What to Do with What You Find

The five-year check may reveal that the marriage is healthier than you realized — that the daily frustrations had obscured a foundation of genuine affection, trust, and shared purpose. If so, name it. Gratitude is not a feeling. It is a practice, and the marriage that practices gratitude is a marriage that reinforces its own health.

The check may reveal problems that are serious but addressable — communication patterns that need repair, intimacy issues that need attention, unresolved conflicts that have been avoided for years and need to be engaged. If so, address them. Now. Not next month, not next year, not when things settle down. The things will not settle down. There will always be a reason to postpone the hard conversation. Do not wait for the reason to run out. The reason will never run out. The marriage might.

The check may reveal that the marriage is in genuine trouble — that the foundation is weaker than either person knew, that the distance between them is greater than adjustment can bridge, that professional help is not optional but urgent. If so, get the help. Not the book. Not the podcast. Not the marriage retreat that costs five hundred dollars and produces a temporary emotional high that fades by Tuesday. A therapist. A skilled, trained, experienced therapist who will sit with you for months and help you do the work that the marriage requires and that you cannot do alone.

And the check may reveal, in rare cases, that the marriage is not viable — that it was built on a foundation that cannot support what a marriage needs, and that the most honest thing both people can do is to name this truth and reckon with its consequences. This is the hardest outcome, and the church must not treat it as the only possible outcome of honest assessment. Most marriages at year five are not beyond repair. They are under-maintained. And under-maintained is a fixable condition.

An Invitation, Not a Judgment

The five-year marriage check is not a test you pass or fail. It is an invitation to look — honestly, without flinching, without the optimistic distortions that protect you from reality and prevent you from change — at what you have built together, and to decide, with open eyes, whether to continue building it.

The couples I admire most are not the couples with the easiest marriages. They are the couples who looked honestly at what they had, named what was working and what was not, and chose — deliberately, sacrificially, with full knowledge of the cost — to keep building. They chose the marriage. Not because it was perfect. Because it was theirs, and because they believed that what could be built on the existing foundation was worth the effort of building it.

Five years is not a milestone. It is a crossroads. And the couple standing at it has a choice: drift forward on inertia, hoping that time will fix what attention has not, or stop, look, assess, and choose the marriage again — this time with the honesty that the first time lacked, because the first time was a promise about the future and this time is a decision about the present.

The decision about the present is always harder. It is also the only one that matters.

chapters.title: The Marriage That Lost Its Friendship
chapters.summary: Before they were lovers, they were friends. Before the mortgage and the children and the routine that replaced conversation, they liked each other. The recovery of friendship may be the most important thing a struggling marriage can do.
chapters.body:
There was a time when they talked. Not about the children's schedules or the broken dishwasher or who was picking up the prescription. They talked about ideas, about memories, about the article one of them read that morning. They talked about nothing in particular for hours, the way you do with someone whose company you enjoy — not because the conversation was important, but because the person was.

They cannot remember when that stopped. It was not a moment. It was an erosion — so gradual that neither of them noticed until the evening came when they sat across from each other at dinner and realized they had nothing to say. Not nothing worth saying. Nothing. The well was dry. The friendship that had been the foundation of the marriage — the thing that made them choose each other in the first place — had been replaced by a management partnership. They were efficient together. They ran the household. They divided the labor. They were, by every functional measure, a successful team. And they were lonely in a way that only people who share a life with someone they no longer know can be lonely.

This is the marriage that lost its friendship. It is not dramatic. There is no affair, no addiction, no crisis that would justify a counselor's appointment or a pastor's intervention. It is simply two people who like each other less than they used to — or, more precisely, two people who have forgotten how to like each other, because liking requires attention, and attention has been directed elsewhere for so long that neither of them knows how to redirect it.

How Friendship Dies in Marriage

The friendship in a marriage dies by neglect, and the neglect has identifiable stages. The first stage is the prioritization of function over connection. This begins, usually, with the arrival of children. The couple that used to spend Saturday mornings in bed talking now spends Saturday mornings at soccer games and grocery stores. The couple that used to cook together now eats in shifts. The couple that used to read aloud to each other now reads separately, in different rooms, after the children are in bed — if they read at all, if they have the energy, if they are not already asleep.

This is understandable. Children require attention, and the attention must come from somewhere. But what the couple does not realize, in those early years of parenting, is that they are making a withdrawal from an account they are not replenishing. The friendship was built by hours of shared attention. It is being starved by the redirection of that attention to the demands of the household. And when the demands eventually subside — when the children are older, when the schedule loosens — the couple discovers that the friendship they assumed would be waiting for them has died in their absence.

The second stage is the replacement of curiosity with assumption. In the early years, you asked your spouse questions because you did not know the answers. What do you think about this? How do you feel about that? What would you do if? Over time, you stop asking because you think you already know. You assume you know what your spouse thinks about politics, about faith, about the neighbor's new car. And in most cases, you are right — you do know. But the act of asking was never primarily about acquiring information. It was about expressing interest. It was the verbal equivalent of turning toward someone and saying, with your attention, "You matter to me. Your inner life is worth my curiosity." When the asking stops, the message that replaces it is: I already know everything about you. There is nothing new to discover. You are a solved equation.

Nobody wants to be a solved equation.

The third stage is the accumulation of unprocessed grievances. Every marriage generates friction, and healthy marriages process the friction through conversation — through the small, ongoing negotiations that keep two people calibrated. But the marriage that has lost its friendship has also lost the channel through which friction is processed. The conversation that should happen — "It bothered me when you said that" — does not happen, because the couple no longer has the relational credit to absorb the vulnerability that honest conversation requires. Instead, the grievances accumulate. They pile up like snow on a roof, invisible from the outside, adding weight that the structure was not designed to carry.

Eventually, the roof collapses — not under the weight of any single grievance, but under the accumulated weight of years of unspoken ones. And both spouses are bewildered, because none of the individual grievances seem heavy enough to explain the collapse. They are not heavy enough. Individually. Together, they are crushing.

What John Gottman Found

The research of John Gottman — the psychologist who has studied marriage with more rigor and over a longer period than anyone else in the field — consistently identifies friendship as the most important predictor of marital satisfaction and stability. Not passion. Not compatibility. Not shared values or shared interests or shared faith. Friendship. The simple, unspectacular reality of two people who know each other, like each other, and turn toward each other when the world turns against them.

Gottman's concept of "bids for connection" is particularly illuminating. A bid is any attempt by one spouse to connect with the other — a comment, a question, a touch, a look. "Look at that bird" is a bid. "How was your meeting?" is a bid. Reaching for your spouse's hand while watching television is a bid. Gottman found that couples who stayed together turned toward their partner's bids 86 percent of the time. Couples who divorced turned toward only 33 percent of the time.

The numbers are stark, but the mechanism is intuitive. Every bid is a test — a small, often unconscious test of whether the other person is available, interested, present. When the bid is met — when the spouse looks at the bird, answers the question, takes the offered hand — the message is: I am here. You are not alone. We are connected. When the bid is ignored — when the spouse does not look up, does not answer, does not take the hand — the message is: you do not matter enough to interrupt what I am doing. And enough of those messages, received over enough years, will kill the friendship as surely as oxygen deprivation kills a flame.

What the Church Can Say

The church has a theology of marriage as covenant, as sacrament, as a reflection of Christ and the church. What it lacks is a theology of marriage as friendship — a framework that takes seriously the daily, unglamorous, absolutely essential practice of liking the person you love.

The Song of Solomon provides the raw material. "This is my beloved and this is my friend," the woman declares. The two categories are not separated. They are held together, and the holding together is the point. The beloved is the friend. The friend is the beloved. The marriage that loses the friendship has not merely lost a convenience. It has lost a constitutive element — the element without which the covenant, however intact, is hollow.

The church should say this: friendship in marriage is not optional. It is not a bonus that some couples enjoy and others manage without. It is the soil in which everything else — sex, parenting, conflict resolution, spiritual growth — takes root. Without it, the marriage can function, but it cannot flourish. And God did not institute marriage so that two people could function together. God said, "It is not good for the man to be alone," and the solution was not a business partner or a roommate. It was a companion. A friend.

The Recovery of Friendship

Friendship in marriage can be recovered, but the recovery requires intentionality that feels, at first, artificial. The couple that has not had a real conversation in months cannot simply decide to start having real conversations. They have to relearn the skill — and it is a skill — of being curious about each other, of turning toward bids, of carving out time that is not functional but relational.

This means dates. Not the performative date night that the church has elevated to a sacrament — not the expensive dinner where both people sit across from each other trying to remember how to talk. Simple dates. A walk. A drive. An errand done together instead of divided for efficiency. The goal is not romance. The goal is proximity without agenda — the condition in which friendship naturally grows.

It means questions. Real questions, not the questions you already know the answers to. "What are you worried about that you have not told me?" "What is the best part of your life right now?" "If you could change one thing about our daily routine, what would it be?" These questions require vulnerability from the asker and the answerer, and vulnerability is the currency of friendship.

It means turning off the screens. The phone, the laptop, the television — these are the enemies of friendship, not because technology is evil but because technology provides an endless supply of stimulation that requires nothing from you. Friendship requires something from you. It requires your attention, your presence, your willingness to be bored together — because boredom, shared, is the precondition for the spontaneous conversation, the unexpected discovery, the moment of connection that no algorithm can engineer.

What Friendship Makes Possible

The marriage that recovers its friendship does not merely become happier. It becomes more resilient. The friendship is the shock absorber — the thing that cushions the marriage against the inevitable impacts of life in a fallen world. The couple that likes each other can survive a financial crisis. The couple that has lost its friendship may not survive a bad week.

Friendship also makes the hard conversations possible. The couple that is friends can say, "I need to tell you something difficult" without the other person bracing for catastrophe. The friendship creates a context of safety — a confidence that the person across from you is for you, not against you, and that the difficult thing they are about to say comes from a place of care rather than contempt.

And friendship makes the marriage worth fighting for. The couple in crisis who can still say, "I like this person — I have forgotten how to show it, but I like who they are" — that couple has something to build on. The couple who cannot say it, who have not liked each other in years, who stay together out of obligation or fear or inertia — that couple has a harder road, though not an impossible one.

The recovery of friendship in marriage is not the recovery of the past. You cannot go back to the people you were when the friendship was new. You can go forward to the people you are now — older, more tired, more complicated, and more in need of a friend than you have ever been.

The friend is there. Across the table. Across the silence. Waiting to be rediscovered.

All it takes is turning toward them. And saying something. Anything. Even: "Look at that bird."

chapters.title: The Marriage That Survives Ministry
chapters.summary: Ministry marriages do not fail because pastors are bad spouses — they fail because the church has built a system that demands the pastor give everything to the congregation and expects the family to survive on the leftovers.
chapters.body:
I need to say something that most pastors will not say publicly, because saying it publicly feels like a confession of weakness, and weakness in ministry is the one thing you are never allowed to show. Here it is: there have been seasons in my ministry when my marriage survived not because of my faithfulness but in spite of my unfaithfulness — not unfaithfulness in the sexual sense, but in the vocational sense. I gave the church my best energy, my best attention, my best emotional presence, and I gave my wife what was left. What was left was not enough. It was never enough.

This is not a unique confession. It is a nearly universal one among pastors, and the fact that it is rarely spoken does not mean it is rarely felt. The Barna Group's 2017 study on pastoral health found that 52 percent of pastors reported that the demands of ministry had a negative effect on their family. The Hartford Institute's research found that 80 percent of pastors believed pastoral ministry negatively affected their families. Francis Schaeffer, reflecting on his own ministry failures, wrote with painful honesty about the gap between the community he preached and the marriage he practiced.

The question is not whether ministry is hard on marriages. The question is why. And the answer is more structural than personal, more systemic than spiritual, more about the way we have designed the pastoral role than about the character of the people who fill it.

The Structural Problem

The modern pastoral role is structurally designed to destroy marriages. This is not an exaggeration. Consider what the role demands: the pastor is expected to be available at all hours for emergencies — hospital visits, suicidal parishioners, marital crises, deaths. The pastor is expected to prepare and deliver multiple sermons per week, each one representing hours of study, writing, and emotional labor. The pastor is expected to attend committee meetings, lead staff, manage budgets, cast vision, respond to criticism, mediate conflict, visit the elderly, counsel the struggling, and show up at every church event with a smile that communicates both warmth and pastoral authority.

The pastor is also expected to have a thriving marriage and well-adjusted children, because these are understood to be qualifications for the role. First Timothy 3:4-5 says that an overseer must "manage his own household well." The congregation reads this as a requirement and then builds a system that makes compliance nearly impossible. We demand the fruit while poisoning the soil.

The structural problem is compounded by the absence of boundaries that would be considered non-negotiable in any other profession. A surgeon does not take calls during surgery. A trial lawyer does not step out of the courtroom to handle a church member's anxiety attack. But the pastor is expected to leave the dinner table when the phone rings, to cancel the anniversary date when a deacon has a crisis, to prioritize the congregation's needs over the family's needs as a demonstration of ministerial faithfulness.

And the spouse — the pastor's spouse — is expected to accept this arrangement without complaint, because the work is "the Lord's work," and who would compete with the Lord? The theological framing of ministry makes it nearly impossible for the spouse to name the deprivation without feeling guilty. How do you say, "I need you to be home tonight" when the alternative is a teenager in the ER? How do you say, "I need your attention" when the alternative is a grieving widow? The pastor's spouse learns, over time, that their needs will always lose the triage, because the congregation's needs are always more urgent, more visible, and more spiritually weighted.

The system is reinforced by a pastoral culture that rewards self-sacrifice and punishes self-care. The pastor who takes a full day off is suspected of laziness. The pastor who goes on vacation without checking email is suspected of disengagement. The pastor who says, "I cannot take that meeting because I have a date with my wife" is suspected of misplaced priorities. The culture of pastoral ministry has confused martyrdom with faithfulness, and the confusion is destroying families.

The Emotional Depletion

The structural demands would be manageable if the emotional toll were acknowledged and addressed. It is not. Ministry is one of the most emotionally intensive professions in existence, and it operates with almost no emotional infrastructure.

Consider what a typical week contains. Monday: debriefing from Sunday, responding to the person offended by the sermon, processing the conversation in the lobby with the couple whose marriage is ending. Tuesday: hospital visit with a dying church member, followed by a staff meeting about budget shortfalls, followed by a counseling session with a man struggling with pornography. Wednesday: midweek teaching, youth group crisis, email from a board member questioning a decision. Thursday: sermon preparation — which is not merely intellectual work but emotional and spiritual labor, the work of wrestling with a text until it yields something true enough to say out loud. Friday: wedding rehearsal, phone call from a church member whose child was just diagnosed with cancer. Saturday: the wedding, followed by a few hours of exhausted presence at home before the cycle begins again on Sunday.

By the time the pastor arrives at the dinner table — if they arrive at the dinner table — they have given away the best of themselves to people who are not their family. The empathy has been spent. The emotional availability has been drained. The capacity to be present, to listen, to engage, to care — the very capacities that the marriage needs most — have been distributed across thirty or forty pastoral interactions, and there is nothing left.

The spouse sees the exhaustion. The spouse understands the demands. The spouse tries to be gracious, patient, supportive. But grace has limits, patience has a shelf life, and support without reciprocity eventually becomes resentment. And the resentment, when it arrives, carries an additional burden of guilt, because the spouse knows they are resenting "God's work," and what kind of person resents God's work?

The kind of person who has been neglected by their spouse for fifteen years while the congregation got the best of them. That kind of person.

The Fishbowl Effect

Ministry marriages carry an additional burden that few other marriages face: they are lived in public. The pastor's marriage is the congregation's property — not legally, but functionally. The congregation watches how the pastor and spouse interact on Sunday mornings. They form opinions about the health of the marriage. They gossip when the spouse seems withdrawn. They expect the marriage to model what the pastor preaches, and when it does not — when the strain shows, when the facade slips, when the marriage looks ordinary rather than exemplary — the judgment arrives.

This public scrutiny makes vulnerability impossible. The pastor cannot stand before the congregation and say, "My marriage is struggling this month." The spouse cannot ask for prayer in the small group without it becoming a talking point in the parking lot. The couple lives inside a performance that they cannot exit, and the performance itself becomes one of the primary sources of marital stress. They are performing intimacy for an audience while the actual intimacy erodes behind the curtain.

The loneliest couple in most churches is the couple in the parsonage. They have access to everyone and intimacy with no one. They know the congregation's secrets but cannot share their own. They carry the weight of the church's dysfunction while pretending their own household is functional. And the pretense, sustained over years, becomes a kind of spiritual sickness — a disease of the soul that masquerades as ministerial faithfulness.

The Theological Distortion

Underneath the structural and emotional problems lies a theological distortion that the church has rarely examined: the idolatry of ministry. The belief — absorbed, not articulated — that pastoral work is the highest calling, that the church's needs are God's needs, and that the family must be sacrificed on the altar of vocational faithfulness.

This is not what Scripture teaches. Scripture teaches that the first institution God created was not the church but the family. Before there was a tabernacle, before there was a temple, before there was a congregation, there was a man and a woman in a garden, called to be one flesh. The family precedes the church in the order of creation, and while I do not want to build an entire theology on chronological priority, the ordering is not accidental. The God who made marriage before He made Israel is a God who does not regard the family as a resource to be consumed by institutional religion.

Jesus Himself modeled something the church has largely ignored: the discipline of withdrawal. He withdrew from the crowds to pray. He withdrew from the demands of ministry to be alone with His Father. He told His disciples, after a period of intense ministry, "Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while" (Mark 6:31). Jesus did not treat every need as a claim on His time. He did not respond to every urgency with immediate availability. He withdrew. He rested. He said no.

The pastor who cannot say no to the congregation for the sake of the marriage has made the congregation an idol. This is an uncomfortable sentence, and I am aware of it. But it is true. The God who called you to ministry is the same God who gave you a spouse, and He did not give you the second to sacrifice for the first.

Eugene Peterson understood this. In "The Pastor," he wrote about his deliberate decision to be home for dinner, to keep Mondays free, to refuse the tyranny of the urgent in favor of the discipline of the important. Peterson was not a lazy pastor. He was a pastor who understood that the rhythms of the pastoral life must include rhythms of absence from the congregation — absence that is not abandonment but stewardship. The pastor who is always available is not being faithful. That pastor is being consumed. And the family that watches the consumption has learned a lesson about the church that will take years to unlearn.

What Must Change

The marriage that survives ministry does not survive by accident. It survives by deliberate, sustained, counter-cultural choices that will cost the pastor something — and the something it costs may be the approval of the congregation that has come to expect unlimited access to their pastor's life.

First, the pastor must establish and enforce boundaries that protect the marriage. This means designated times that are non-negotiable — date nights that do not get cancelled for committee meetings, vacations that do not include a laptop and a sermon outline, evenings that are given to the family without the phone on the table. The congregation will not like this. Some will interpret it as a lack of dedication. The pastor must be willing to pay that price, because the alternative — the slow erosion of the marriage in the name of ministerial availability — is a price that is too high.

Second, the pastor must find safe spaces for their own vulnerability. This means a counselor, a spiritual director, a small circle of trusted friends outside the congregation who can hold what the pastor cannot hold alone. The pastor who tries to be the sole emotional caregiver for a congregation while receiving no care themselves is a pastor who will either burn out, blow up, or both. And when the pastor burns out or blows up, the marriage is usually the first casualty.

Third, the congregation must change its expectations. This is the hardest shift, because it requires the congregation to see the pastor as a human being rather than a spiritual utility. The pastor is not a vending machine that dispenses pastoral care on demand. The pastor is a person with a body that gets tired, a heart that gets wounded, and a marriage that needs the same investment that every marriage needs. Congregations that demand unlimited access to their pastor are not being faithful. They are being consumptive. And the consumption will eventually destroy the person they claim to need.

Fourth, and this is the thing I have learned most slowly: the pastor must bring the same pastoral skill to their own marriage that they bring to everyone else's. The irony of pastoral ministry is that the pastor is often the most skilled relational person in the congregation and the least skilled relational person in their own home. They listen to parishioners with full attention and scroll through their phone while their spouse is talking. They counsel couples with empathy and patience and argue with their own spouse with impatience and defensiveness. They know, theoretically, what a healthy marriage requires. They fail, practically, to practice it where it matters most.

The marriage that survives ministry is not the marriage that sacrifices everything for the church. It is the marriage that recognizes that the church does not own the pastor, that the family is not an obstacle to ministry but the first ministry, and that the God who called the pastor to serve is the same God who commanded the pastor to love — and the love starts at home.

I have learned this slowly, imperfectly, with more failure than I want to admit. My marriage has survived ministry not because I got this right but because grace covered the years when I got it wrong. That grace does not excuse the wrong. It redeems it. And the redemption calls me not to repeat the pattern but to break it — to be the pastor who goes home, who puts the phone down, who looks his wife in the eye and says, "You are not second. You were never supposed to be second. And I am sorry for every season when I made you feel like you were."

I think of the pastors I know who lost their marriages. Not one of them lost it because they were lazy. They lost it because they were faithful — faithful to the wrong thing, or faithful to the right thing in the wrong proportion. They gave everything to the church and assumed the family would understand. The family understood for a while. Then the family stopped understanding. Then the family left.

The tragedy is not that these men were bad pastors. Many of them were extraordinary pastors — gifted preachers, compassionate counselors, visionary leaders. The tragedy is that the very gifts that made them effective in ministry were the gifts they withheld from their marriages. The empathy they showed the grieving widow, they did not show their wives. The patience they extended to the difficult deacon, they did not extend to their children. The presence they brought to the hospital bedside, they did not bring to the dinner table. The ministry received their best. The family received what remained.

The ministry will survive your absence for an evening. Your marriage may not survive your absence for a decade. Choose accordingly.

chapters.title: The Married Doubter: When One Spouse Loses Faith
chapters.summary: You said your vows to two believers, and now there is only one. This is for the marriage where faith has quietly become a fault line.
chapters.body:
You built a life on a shared faith, and now that foundation has shifted. Maybe you are the one who has lost your faith, watching your spouse's hurt and confusion and fear, feeling like a stranger in your own marriage, wondering if the person who married you can still love the person you are becoming. Or maybe you are the one still believing, watching your husband or wife walk away from the God you built your home around, feeling abandoned in a way that has no name, grieving a person who is still sitting across the dinner table. Either way, something you assumed would always be shared has become the thing that divides you, and the marriage is straining under a weight neither of you planned for.

I want to be careful here, because both of you are hurting and the church usually only speaks to one of you. It tells the believing spouse to stand firm and pray, and it tells the doubting spouse, implicitly or explicitly, that they are the problem. I am not going to do that. I am going to speak to both people in this marriage, because there are two souls in this story, and both of them are afraid, and both of them deserve better than the sides they are being pushed onto.

To the spouse who still believes

Your grief is real, and I want to name it before I say anything else, because most people around you are treating this as a theological problem to be solved rather than a loss to be mourned. You are grieving. The person you married, the one you dreamed with about raising your children in the faith, about growing old in the same pew, about a shared eternity, has changed in the one way you never prepared for. That is a genuine bereavement, even though they are still alive and still yours. Do not let anyone rush you past the grief or shame you for feeling it.

But I have to give you a warning, gently, because I have watched believing spouses lose their marriages not to the doubt but to their response to the doubt. The temptation is to turn your marriage into a mission field. To argue. To leave apologetics books on the nightstand. To turn every conversation into an altar call. To make your spouse a project. I understand the impulse. It comes from love and from fear. But it does not work, and worse, it often drives the doubting spouse further away, because now they do not just doubt God, they feel judged and cornered by the person who is supposed to love them most. The apostle Peter addressed exactly this situation, married believers with unbelieving spouses, and his counsel is stunning. He said the unbelieving spouse may be won "without a word" by the conduct of the believer (1 Peter 3:1). Without a word. Not by argument. By a life so full of grace that it makes the faith attractive rather than defensive. Your job is not to win the debate. Your job is to love your spouse so well that your faith becomes the most compelling thing in the house.

You cannot argue your spouse back to God. But you can love them in a way that makes God look real. Choose the second. The first has buried more marriages than it has saved.

There is a fear underneath your grief that you may not have named, and I want to name it for you so it stops working in the dark. You are afraid that if you stop pushing, you are giving up on your spouse's soul, that gentleness is a betrayal of the truth, that a loving God requires you to fight harder for their return. Hear me carefully. The pressure you feel to save your spouse is not from God. God is not anxious. He is not wringing His hands hoping you will land the right argument before it is too late. Your spouse's soul is not finally in your hands; it is in His, and He loves them more than you do, which is a sentence worth sitting with because it is almost impossible to believe when you love someone this much. Your job is not to be their savior. It is to be their spouse, faithful and kind, and to trust the actual Savior with the part you were never strong enough to carry anyway.

To the spouse who is losing faith

You are not a villain, and you are probably being treated like one. Your doubt is likely honest, arrived at through real questions or real wounds, and you did not choose it to hurt anyone. Watching your spouse's pain is its own kind of agony. You feel guilty for something you cannot help, judged for being honest, and increasingly like a foreigner in a marriage that used to feel like home. I see you. Your integrity in not faking a faith you no longer feel is worth something, even if no one around you is saying so.

But I have to ask something of you too, because a marriage has two people and both bear responsibility for its care. Do not let your doubt become contempt. It is easy, when you have moved away from a belief, to start seeing your spouse's faith as foolish, to grow impatient with their grief, to treat their fear as irrational. That contempt will kill your marriage faster than the doubt ever could. The researcher John Gottman, who has studied thousands of married couples across decades at the University of Washington, identified contempt as the single strongest predictor of divorce, the acid that dissolves a marriage from within. Your spouse is not stupid for believing. They are grieving a real loss, the loss of the shared faith you both once had. Honor that grief the way you want them to honor your doubt. And do not, in your certainty that you have seen through the faith, become as dogmatic in your unbelief as you accuse them of being in their belief. Doubt held with humility is honest. Doubt held with contempt is just a new fundamentalism.

The marriage is not the theology

Here is the thing that can hold your marriage together while the faith question remains unresolved, and I say this as a pastor who has married and buried and counseled people for fifteen years. Your marriage is not primarily a shared set of beliefs. It is a covenant between two people. You did not marry a doctrinal statement. You married a person, and that person is still there, still the one you chose, still worthy of the vow you made. The vow said for better or for worse. Nobody puts this in their wedding vows, but this is the worse. This is exactly the kind of unforeseen weight the covenant was built to carry.

The temptation on both sides is to treat the faith difference as the whole marriage, to let it colonize every conversation and every interaction until you are no longer a husband and wife but two positions in an argument. Resist that. You are more than your beliefs about God, both of you. You still share children, a history, a home, a thousand ordinary acts of love. Do not let the one area of difference consume the many areas of union. Protect the marriage as a marriage while the faith question works itself out, and it may take years, and it may not resolve the way either of you wants. A marriage can hold two people who disagree about the largest thing, if they refuse to let the disagreement become their whole identity as a couple.

You married a person, not a doctrinal statement. The person is still there. The vow was built to carry exactly this weight. Do not set it down because the theology got hard.

I want to speak practically about the thing that will actually decide whether your marriage survives this, and it is not the theology. It is how you handle the daily friction the difference creates. Church on Sunday. What you tell the children. The prayer before dinner that one of you no longer means. The holidays. The friends who ask. These small collisions, if they are handled with contempt or ultimatums, will grind the marriage down long before any grand crisis of belief. If they are handled with negotiation and tenderness and a shared commitment to protect the union above winning the point, the marriage can absorb an astonishing amount of difference. Decide together, before the collisions come, that you will treat each other as allies working out a hard situation, not as opponents in a war of worldviews. The couples who survive this are not the ones who resolve the theology. They are the ones who refuse to let the theology make them enemies at the kitchen table.

Do not force the ending

To the believing spouse, do not conclude that a spouse who has lost faith is a spouse you are permitted or required to leave. Paul addressed this directly. "If any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her. For the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife" (1 Corinthians 7:12 through 14). Your presence in the marriage is not compromised by your spouse's doubt. It may be the very thing God uses. And to the doubting spouse, do not conclude that because you have changed, the honest thing is to blow up the life you built. Honesty about your beliefs does not require dishonoring your covenant. You can be truthful about your doubt and faithful to your marriage at the same time. These are not in conflict, though the pressure will tempt you to treat them as if they are.

And to both of you, get help that honors both people. Find a counselor, ideally one who understands both the faith dimension and the marital dynamics, who will not simply take the side of belief or the side of doubt. This is not something most couples can carry alone, and reaching for help is not a sign the marriage is failing. It is a sign you are fighting for it. If the strain has grown so heavy that either of you is falling into a darkness that makes you not want to be here anymore, please reach out tonight. In the United States you can call or text 988. A marriage under this weight is worth protecting, and so is each of the two lives in it.

The verdict

One of you lost the faith you both once shared, and it has become a fault line running through your home. But a fault line is not a divorce, and a difference is not the end. The marriage you built was never only a shared theology. It was a covenant between two people who chose each other, and that covenant was designed to carry weights neither of you could foresee. This is one of them. It is heavy. It is not necessarily fatal.

Believing spouse, love your husband or wife without a word, so well that your faith is the most compelling thing in the house, and stop trying to win a debate you can only lose by fighting. Doubting spouse, hold your doubt with humility instead of contempt, and honor the grief of the person watching you change. Both of you, protect the marriage as a marriage while the question of God works itself out slowly, over years, in ways you cannot control. You do not have to agree about the largest thing to keep the vow you made. You only have to keep choosing the person you married, the one still sitting across the table, still worth the promise. The faith may return or it may not. The love does not have to leave with it. Guard that. It is the thing you can still choose today.

chapters.title: The Sexless Marriage Nobody Talks About
chapters.summary: The absence of physical intimacy in a marriage is not a punchline. It is a wound that both spouses carry in silence, and the church's refusal to address it has left generations without language for what they are losing.
chapters.body:
They sit in the pew on Sunday morning, close enough that their shoulders touch. They look, to anyone watching, like a couple. And they are a couple — legally, domestically, in every external measure. They share a mortgage and a minivan and a last name. But they have not touched each other in months. Some of them have not touched each other in years. And neither of them knows how to talk about it — not to each other, not to their friends, and certainly not to their pastor.

The sexless marriage is one of the most common and least discussed realities in the American church. Researchers define it clinically — fewer than ten sexual encounters per year — but the clinical definition misses the lived experience, which is not primarily about frequency but about rejection, longing, shame, and the slow death of something that was supposed to be a gift.

The church has two modes when it comes to sex in marriage: celebration and prohibition. Before marriage, sex is forbidden. After marriage, sex is a blessing, a gift, a sacred act of union. The wedding night is the great transition — from no to yes, from sin to sacrament. But the church has almost nothing to say about the marriage in which the yes never came, or came and then stopped, or came with so much complication that it barely felt like a gift at all.

This silence has consequences. The spouse who desires physical intimacy and does not receive it carries a shame that has no outlet. The spouse who cannot offer physical intimacy — for reasons that range from trauma to medication to simple loss of desire — carries a guilt that has no relief. And between them, the silence grows, filling the space where honesty should be.

What We Refuse to Name

The first thing the church must do is name the problem honestly. A sexless marriage is not a minor inconvenience. It is a significant deprivation — for both spouses, regardless of who desires more and who desires less. Paul wrote to the Corinthians that married couples should not deprive one another except by mutual consent for a limited time. The church has used this passage to guilt reluctant spouses into compliance, which is a grotesque misreading. But the passage contains a genuine insight: physical intimacy in marriage is not optional. It is constitutive. It is part of what makes a marriage a marriage rather than a partnership or a friendship or a cohabitation arrangement.

This does not mean that every spouse is entitled to sex on demand. It means that both spouses are entitled to a marriage in which physical intimacy is present, valued, and mutually sought — even if the seeking is difficult, even if the intimacy looks different from what either person imagined, even if the path to it requires more honesty than either person wants to offer.

The reluctant spouse is not the villain. The desiring spouse is not the victim. These are two people caught in a dynamic that neither of them chose and neither of them knows how to change. The church's job is not to assign blame. It is to provide a framework — theological, pastoral, practical — for two people to talk about the most intimate dimension of their life together without shame.

The Roots of Sexual Withdrawal

Sexual withdrawal in marriage has causes, and the causes matter. They are not excuses. They are explanations, and explanations are the beginning of change.

For some spouses, the withdrawal is rooted in trauma. Sexual abuse in childhood, assault in adolescence, a previous relationship in which sex was coerced or punishing — these experiences do not disappear at the altar. They follow the survivor into the marriage bed, and they surface in ways that are confusing to both spouses. The trauma survivor may want intimacy desperately and find themselves unable to receive it. Their body freezes. Their mind disconnects. The very act that is supposed to express love triggers a cascade of fear responses that have nothing to do with their spouse and everything to do with what happened before their spouse existed.

For others, the withdrawal is medical. Antidepressants suppress desire with a reliability that no one warns patients about until it is too late. Hormonal changes after childbirth, during perimenopause, or as a side effect of other treatments can reduce desire to near zero. Chronic pain makes the physical act of sex difficult or impossible. These are not choices. They are conditions, and the church that treats them as spiritual failures — as a lack of willingness to give one's body to one's spouse — adds cruelty to suffering.

For still others, the withdrawal is relational. It is the accumulated residue of years of unresolved conflict, emotional distance, criticism, contempt, or neglect. The spouse who has been belittled at the dinner table cannot be expected to open themselves in the bedroom. The body keeps score. It registers every dismissive comment, every eye roll, every evening spent in separate rooms staring at separate screens. And eventually it says no — not as a punishment, but as a protection.

And for some, the withdrawal is simply the mystery of desire — that desire has its own logic, its own seasons, its own stubborn refusal to be summoned on command. The church that insists desire is a choice — that you can decide to want your spouse — is speaking a language that does not correspond to how human beings actually work. Desire is not a faucet. You cannot turn it on by trying harder.

The Spouse Who Waits

The spouse who desires intimacy and does not receive it inhabits a particular kind of loneliness. It is not the loneliness of being alone. It is the loneliness of being with someone — sleeping next to someone, sharing a life with someone — and feeling untouched. Unwanted. Invisible.

This spouse often carries shame about their desire. The culture sends contradictory messages: men are supposed to want sex all the time, which means that the man in a sexless marriage feels like a failure; women are not supposed to want sex as much as men, which means that the woman in a sexless marriage feels like a deviant. Both of these scripts are false, and both cause real damage.

The desiring spouse may begin to question their attractiveness, their worth, their identity. If my spouse does not want me, what does that say about me? This question, asked in enough silent moments, becomes a conviction: I am not enough. I am not desirable. Something is wrong with me. And the longer the sexlessness continues, the deeper the conviction roots.

The church must speak to this spouse without patronizing them. You are not wrong to want physical intimacy with the person you married. Your desire is not excessive or sinful or needy. It is the desire that the covenant itself creates — the longing for the union that the vows promised. The absence of that union is a real loss, and you are allowed to grieve it.

The Spouse Who Cannot

The spouse who withholds intimacy — and I use that word carefully, because "withhold" implies agency, and many of these spouses do not experience themselves as withholding anything — carries their own burden. They know what their spouse wants. They know they are not providing it. And they feel, most days, like a failure — or worse, like a fraud. They stood at the altar and promised themselves to this person, body and soul, and their body is not keeping the promise their mouth made.

The guilt is corrosive. It manifests as defensiveness — "Why is sex the only thing that matters to you?" — or as avoidance — staying up late, going to bed early, engineering the schedule so that opportunities for intimacy never arise. These are not strategies of cruelty. They are strategies of shame. The spouse who avoids intimacy is often avoiding the reminder of their own inadequacy.

The church must speak to this spouse with equal honesty and equal compassion. You are not broken. You are not failing at marriage because your body or your desire does not cooperate with your intentions. But you owe your spouse the truth about what you are experiencing — not performance, not excuses, but the vulnerable, frightening truth. "I do not know why I cannot want this. I am sorry. I want to find out." That sentence, spoken honestly, is more intimate than any physical act.

The Path Forward

There is no formula for restoring sexual intimacy to a marriage that has lost it. Anyone who offers you five steps is selling something. But there are practices — honest, difficult, slow practices — that create the conditions in which intimacy can grow.

The first is naming. Say what is happening. Out loud. To each other. "We have not been intimate in four months, and I need to talk about why." This sentence is terrifying. It is also the door through which every other conversation must pass. The sexless marriage that remains sexless usually does so because both spouses have agreed, implicitly, never to name what is happening. Breaking that agreement is the first act of intimacy — the intimacy of truth.

The second is curiosity. Not accusation — curiosity. "What happens for you when I initiate?" "What would feel safe?" "What are you afraid of?" These questions require the desiring spouse to set aside their hurt long enough to listen. They require the reluctant spouse to set aside their shame long enough to answer. Both of these are acts of tremendous courage.

The third is professional help. A good therapist — specifically, a therapist trained in sexual health, not just general marital counseling — can name what the couple cannot name. They can identify patterns, address trauma, explore medical factors, and provide a framework for the conversation that neither spouse can provide on their own. The church that refuses to recommend therapy because it believes prayer should be sufficient is not protecting the sanctity of marriage. It is abandoning couples to a problem they cannot solve alone.

The fourth is patience. Sexual intimacy, once lost, does not return quickly. The couple that expects resolution in weeks will be disappointed. The recovery is measured in months, sometimes years — in small gestures, tentative approaches, setbacks that feel like failures but are actually part of the process. The couple needs to know that the process itself is the faithfulness. The willingness to keep showing up, to keep having the hard conversation, to keep reaching across the distance — that willingness is the covenant in action.

What the Church Must Say

The church must say what it has been afraid to say: that the absence of sexual intimacy in marriage is a serious matter that deserves serious pastoral attention. Not a joke. Not a punchline. Not a footnote in a sermon about something else. A serious matter.

The church must stop treating sex as a reward for spiritual maturity and start treating it as a dimension of the relationship that, like every other dimension, is subject to brokenness, requires grace, and demands honest engagement. The couple in the sexless marriage is not less spiritual than the couple with a flourishing sex life. They are carrying a wound that the church should help them tend, not a sin the church should help them confess.

And the church must make room for the grief. The spouse who has not been touched in years is grieving something real — the loss of a dimension of marriage that they were told would be a gift and that has become an absence. The church that cannot sit with that grief — that rushes to fix it or minimize it or spiritualize it — is not serving these marriages. It is abandoning them.

The sexless marriage is a crisis of intimacy, and the church that claims to know something about intimacy — with God, with neighbor, with spouse — must find the courage to enter this crisis with honesty, compassion, and the willingness to stay for as long as the healing takes.

Which is usually longer than anyone wants it to be.

chapters.title: The Theology of Covenant Marriage
chapters.summary: Marriage is not a contract between two consumers shopping for satisfaction — it is a covenant between two sinners binding themselves to a promise that will outlast every feeling they brought to the altar.
chapters.body:
The most dangerous thing that has happened to marriage in the modern West is not the sexual revolution. It is not no-fault divorce. It is not the redefinition of the institution in law or culture. The most dangerous thing is that we stopped understanding what kind of thing marriage is. We turned a covenant into a contract, and then we wondered why it kept breaking.

A contract is an exchange of goods and services between two parties who retain their autonomy. If one party fails to deliver, the other is released. A covenant is something else entirely. A covenant is an exchange of selves. It does not say, "I will give you this as long as you give me that." It says, "I am yours. Period. The terms do not change when the feelings do." The entire biblical narrative — from Eden to Sinai to Calvary — runs on covenant. And marriage, in Scripture, is not merely an illustration of that narrative. It is one of its primary theaters.

I have performed more than a hundred weddings in fifteen years of ministry. I have watched couples stand at the altar in the full blaze of romantic certainty, voices steady, eyes locked, utterly convinced that their love is the kind that will not falter. I have sat with some of those same couples five years later in my office, the certainty gone, the voices unsteady, asking whether God would really hold them to promises they made when they did not know what the promises would cost. The answer to that question requires a theology of covenant, and the church has largely failed to provide one.

We live in a culture that treats every relationship as provisional. Dating apps have encoded optionality into the mechanics of romance — there is always another profile, another possibility, another person who might be a better fit. This consumer logic does not evaporate at the altar. It follows people into their marriages, whispering that commitment is conditional, that satisfaction is the metric, and that a better option might be one swipe away. The covenant cuts against this logic with the full force of the biblical tradition, and the cut is meant to draw blood.

The Ancient Near Eastern Background

To understand biblical covenant, you must understand what covenants meant in the ancient world before Israel adapted the form for its own purposes. In the ancient Near East, a covenant — Hebrew berith — was the most solemn form of agreement two parties could enter. The Hittite suzerainty treaties of the second millennium BCE established a pattern: a powerful king would bind himself to a vassal, not because the vassal had earned the relationship, but because the king chose to extend it. The treaty included a historical prologue recounting what the king had done, stipulations for the vassal's conduct, blessings for faithfulness, curses for unfaithfulness, and a ceremony involving the cutting of animals.

That last detail matters more than it might seem. The Hebrew phrase for making a covenant is karat berith — literally, "to cut a covenant." In Genesis 15, when God makes His covenant with Abraham, the patriarch cuts animals in half and arranges the pieces in two rows with a path between them. In the ancient world, both parties walked between the pieces, symbolically saying, "May I be torn apart like these animals if I break this covenant." But in Genesis 15, something extraordinary happens. God alone — represented as a smoking fire pot and a blazing torch — passes between the pieces. Abraham does not walk. God walks alone. The covenant is unilateral. God binds Himself, absorbs the risk, and stakes His own integrity on the promise.

This is the theological DNA that enters every biblical covenant, including marriage. And the church has largely forgotten it.

The covenant at Sinai deepened the pattern. In Exodus 24, Moses takes the blood of the sacrifice and throws half on the altar (representing God) and half on the people. The blood binds both parties. It is visceral, physical, unforgettable. The people who stood in that blood never forgot what they had entered. The modern wedding, with its flowers and photographers and reception playlists, has sanitized the ceremony to the point where the gravity of what is happening — two people binding their lives together in a bond that God Himself witnesses — is almost entirely obscured. We have made the covenant pretty. It was never meant to be pretty. It was meant to be permanent.

Marriage as Divine Pedagogy

The prophet Hosea received the strangest ministry assignment in all of Scripture: marry a woman who will be unfaithful to you. Gomer's infidelity was not incidental to Hosea's prophetic work. It was the prophetic work. God used a broken marriage to teach Israel something about divine love that no sermon could have communicated — that the covenant partner does not leave when the other partner wanders. That faithfulness is not contingent on reciprocity. That love, in the biblical sense, is not an emotion that arises in response to the beloved's worthiness but a decision that persists in the face of the beloved's unworthiness.

Jeremiah extended this imagery. Ezekiel made it graphic — startlingly, uncomfortably graphic, in ways that most preachers skip over. By the time Paul writes Ephesians 5, he is working with a metaphorical tradition that has been building for a thousand years: marriage is an icon of the relationship between God and God's people. "This mystery is profound," Paul writes, "and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church." The profundity is not merely spiritual. It is structural. Marriage, in the biblical imagination, is designed to function as a living parable — a daily, embodied demonstration of what it looks like when two parties bind themselves together in a bond that neither party can unilaterally dissolve.

This is why the stakes are so high. Not because God is a rule-maker who enjoys holding people to uncomfortable commitments. But because marriage is the primary institution through which human beings learn what covenant love feels like from the inside. Every other covenant in Scripture — the Abrahamic, the Mosaic, the Davidic, the New — uses marriage as its interpretive key. If you gut the institution of its covenantal content, you lose the analogy, and with it, the capacity to understand the God who made it.

Karl Barth understood this with characteristic precision. In Church Dogmatics III/4, he argued that the covenant relationship between God and humanity is not merely illustrated by marriage but is the archetype of which marriage is the ectype.
